records.text: estoring the consumption tax rate once it has been lowered would likely require considerable political effort, meaning there is a high risk that the cut would become permanent. It took 17 years to raise the consumption tax rate from 5% (in 1997) to 8% (in 2014). If a permanent tax cut was combined with increased defense spending and rising interest payments, the government debt-to-GDP ratio could shift to a long-term upward trajectory. However, uncertainty remains around the process leading to the realization of a tax cut. Prime Minister Takaichi has stated that she would not issue deficit-financing bonds to fund the tax cut, which means that ¥5 tn in funding would need to be secured through tax increases (including the reduction of special tax measures mentioned by PM Takaichi) or spending cuts. However, the difficulty of reaching a consensus in a cross-party National Council on tax increases or spending cuts would likely be high, and thus it may take longer than expected to finalize a tax cut plan. During both the bursting of the Tech Bubble and the GFC, US 10-year yields dropped close to 200bp. However, currently US 10-year yields are much lower compared to the Tech Bubble, suggesting a potentially smaller buffer. Also, during the GFC, while bond yields were comparable to now, breakeven inflation fell sharply due to deflation fears — this might be less likely this time due to lingering inflation fears. Fiscal policy risks and bond supply (potentially with less Fed QE) might also mean yield curves are steepening more in the next recession. Yield curves globally have already steepened materially due to a combination of higher inflation volatility, fiscal policy concerns and bond supply. A combination of more expansive fiscal policy globally, more recently in Germany and Japan, as well as concerns about fiscal dominance, might keep upward pressure on longer-dated bond yields in the medium term. This, coupled with potentially more inflation volatility, could result in lower Sharpe ratios for bonds — the risk parity boom since the late 1990s was driven both by more negative equity/bond correlations and strong risk-adjusted returns through cycle. Also, for some bond markets, FX depreciation, especially during ‘risk off’ episodes, might erode returns for foreign investors — as we have discussed before, this might lead to more of a home bias for bond investors. Private borrowing costs would be impacted too, as well as risky assets. Bonus track: the role of the dollar A final word on the implications for the dollar. We expect a somewhat weaker dollar from here but there is a limit to how much the USD can weaken in real terms. The market consensus is that the dollar is highly overvalued in real terms. However, a substantial real depreciation of the US dollar is not sustainable. There is simply not enough growth in Euro Area, UK, Japan and China to tolerate their currencies appreciating by that much in real terms. Such a real appreciation would trigger a global recession that would restore the dollar’s strength. US Fiscal profligacy requires a weaker dollar in nominal terms but not necessarily in real terms as most developed countries face similar fiscal issues. However, if the independence of the Fed were to be undermined, we should see a weaker USD in nominal terms and eventually higher inflation in the US. Although, to be clear, yesterday’s increase in initial claims also may just be temporary due to the snow and cold weather disruptions in the US. records.text: Implications of holding 2/3 of Lower House Seats The ruling coalition has secured a “supermajority” of over two-thirds (310 seats) of the Lower House seats. A supermajority allows a bill to be passed even if it is rejected by the Upper House; the bill can be sent back to the Lower House and enacted if it is passed again by a two-thirds or greater majority. There were several examples of this during 2007-2009, when bills rejected by the Upper House, where the ruling coalition lacked a majority, were re-passed and enacted in the Lower House, where it held a two-thirds majority. With a supermajority, the rules allow for many bills to be passed by a re-vote in the Lower House, even with a minority in the Upper House. However, frequent use of this measure to pass legislation could give the impression that the ruling coalition is running the Diet in a heavy-handed manner, without considering the voices of others. We believe that, as in the past when the ruling coalition held a supermajority, the ruling coalition would basically maintain a stance of cooperating with the opposition on a policy-by-policy basis, as needed. Nevertheless, a supermajority would likely provide additional momentum for the Takaichi administration to implement its medium- to long-term proactive fiscal agenda. We have repeatedly been asked over the past few weeks whether there might be a risk of Japanese investors selling US Treasuries for JGBs now that yields on the latter have improved to such a degree. In other words, many overseas investors appear increasingly concerned that rises in Japanese interest rates could trigger repatriation flows sufficient to impact negatively on other rates markets (we discussed this theme in detail in No symptoms of Japanese repatriation so far ). Long-term interest rates have surged particularly sharply in Japan on concerns that JPY depreciation might be increasing the risk of the BoJ falling behind the curve, which has perhaps led many to believe that the US might now be more inclined to cooperate with action to prevent a spillover effect of a JGB yield sell-off to UST yields via the FX channel. records.text: e Fed’s balance sheet would be smaller, reserves would not need to change in that scenario, and the Treasury’s interest payments to the Fed would be lower. Exhibit 2: It would take approximately 8 years for the Fed's mortgage portfolio to be cut in half to ~1trn$. Reducing the size of the Treasury General Account (TGA) by will not alter reserves in the banking system, but still lower the balance sheet. Source: FRB, Morgan Stanley Research A key question, though, is whether the smaller Fed balance sheet implies higher market rates, especially at the longer end of the curve. The critical but perhaps counterintuitive answer is “not necessarily.” If the shrinking of the balance sheet comes from passive runoff of the Fed’s Treasuries, that extra supply of Treasuries goes to the market, but only through Treasury debt auctions. The Treasury, not the Fed, would determine the maturity distribution of Treasuries that the market has to buy. The recent refunding announcement was important, because Treasury reiterated its preference in the near term to fund itself in the near term more through bills and to avoid increasing coupon auction sizes for some time. If that patter were to continue, the Treasuries that the Fed relinquishes might get refunded to the markets through relatively short-dated paper, limiting any upward pressure on longer-term rates.

records.text: Second part of report title D EEP D I V E DEEP DIVE Disinflation postponed, again: The last time the US economy looked to be experiencing a clear state of disinflation was H1 2024. Since then, core inflation has been more range-bound than converging to official targets, hovering around 3% y/y as the narrative has rotated from supply-chain normalization to stickiness in services to tariff impacts. Our base case is that this pattern extends in 2026. We anticipate another year where the level of core inflation feels stable even as the drivers rotate beneath the surface. Conceptually, we see 2026 core inflation as the net result of three forces: (1) goods firming, as remaining tariff pass-through and related markup dynamics prevent prices from returning to the pre-Covid disinflation regime; (2) shelter cooling, as the post-pandemic rent cycle unwinds further but increasingly approaches its “last mile”; and (3) services persistence, where inflation is more likely to drift than to snap back to 2% due to the combination of low-frequency price resets, non-market pricing, and a Phillips curve that appears meaningfully nonlinear. Near term, risks skew inflationary. Cyclical momentum in the economy is strong and policy could become more supportive via incremental fiscal and/or credit easing as November’s midterm elections approach. Supply is no longer accelerating, while at the same time demand for rental units is far from collapsing. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 7 investor skepticism that further front-end rate convergence is the most likely catalyst for JPY strength. Rather, they tend to point to a reversal of the current themes. Investors say they are watching bond market signals in Japan closely – a flattening of the nominal curve led by a reduction in term premium and breakevens, in their eyes, would presage further JPY strength. But carry remains important here too. If FX vol is insufficiently high, then even fundamental forces supporting JPY may see limited investor appetite to participate. Thus, a pick-up in implied/realized volatility, in many investors' eyes, would incentivize greater participation in a USD/JPY downside trade, leading to greater confidence in the price action.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 13 Survey of Professional Forecasters. The Philadelphia Fed's survey has been run since 1968, and the Fed looks at it for its measures of growth, inflation, and labor market expectations. In the 4Q survey, median estimates of 2026 growth were 1.8%, up 0.2 pct pt from the prior quarter's forecast. The unemployment rate would average 4.5%, on payroll growth of 86k per month. If the polls are accurate the ruling coalition appears to be in a position to secure at least a 'stable majority' (243 seats or more) with potential to secure an 'absolute stable majority' (261 seats or more). A stable majority refers to a situation in which the ruling parties hold all chairperson posts of the 17 standing committees in the Lower House and hold half of the committee seats. The number of committee members allocated to each parliamentary group is proportional to its strength. If a bill is put to a vote in committee and the ruling and opposition camps split evenly, the committee chair casts the deciding vote, allowing the bill to pass. An absolute stable majority means that the ruling parties not only secure all committee chair posts but also hold a majority of seats on every standing committee. This enables the ruling bloc to pass bills without cooperation from the opposition. Because substantive deliberations on legislation take place within committees in Japan, their composition is critically important. records.text: M Foundation 12 The public pension funds conduct an annual check to assess whether the investment environment assumptions used to formulate the current basic portfolio remain consistent with reality, and they could revise the basic portfolio depending on the outcome of that review. However, such intermediate changes have never happened before. Meanwhile, the public pension funds can raise their allocation to domestic bonds at their discretion to as high as 31% (25%+6%), which can generate near JPY 9-10 trillion rebalancing to domestic bonds. That said, the public pension program’s current basic portfolio has been designed with a view to generate a real return of +1.9% over nominal wage growth rate with minimum risk. Expected returns on JGBs have indeed risen of late, but even 40-year JGBs still fall short of delivering above the real expected return (assuming that nominal wage growth is around 3.0%). On top of that, given the sharp rise in JGB volatility in recent months, JGBs are not particularly attractive from a risk adjusted return perspective. We thus consider speculation about the possibility of Japan’s pension program increasing its exposure to JGBs (beyond standard rebalancing needs) to be a little overblown, and expect that allocations will continue to depend mostly on the relative performance of each asset class. Morgan The BoE kept rates on hold at 3.75% at the February meeting this week but both the vote split and the overall guidance was more dovish than expected. At the last BoE meet- ing in December the BoE had delivered a 25bp cut with a 5-4 vote and this month the vote was also 5-4 to keep rates on hold, with Breeden, Dhingra, Ramsden and Taylor all dissent- ing dovishly vs. consensus expectations for a 7-2 dovish dissent. The statement highlighted that risks from inflation persistence had become less pronounced with risks to inflation from weaker demand and a loosening in the labour market remained. The forecast revisions were also more dovish with a larger than expected downward revision to growth (1Q26 from 1.1% to 0.8%), a higher peak in the unemployment rate (5.3%) and CPI inflation close to 2.0% from 2Q26. The statement retains a bias to ease but the language was tweaked with the wording around “gradual” easing removed with the guidance stating “... Bank Rate is likely to be reduced further. Judgements around further policy easing will become a closer call. The extent and timing of further easing in monetary policy will depend on the evolution of the outlook for inflation”. (3) Are elevated equity valuations likely to weigh on returns in 2026? Elevated equity valuations might be a speed limit for returns in the medium term but with favourable macro conditions they are a less binding constraint near term. Valuations for risky assets broadly are elevated, which is typical in a late-cycle backdrop with low unemployment rates and high profit margins (Exhibit 13). And with higher bond yields equity risk premia are the lowest in 20 years — the same is true with credit spreads, which are particularly tight. But while that may present a speed limit for equity returns in the medium term, it might be a less binding constraint in the near term as long as macro conditions remain favourable. records.text: United Kingdom Outlook March on The BoE held policy unchanged but gave a dovish lean to its guidance, with a minority of four members preferring a 25bp cut. We believe they will fall over the coming months back to levels consistent with realised inflation at 2%. • Surveys also continued to support a pickup in activity in the first quarter of 2026. Bank of England meeting increases our conviction in a March cut The Bank of England held Bank Rate at 3.75% at its February meeting, as we had expected. A key development is the narrowing performance gap between the core and periphery economies. The core, particularly Germany, is showing signs of bottoming out, supported by expectations of a significant fiscal boost. In contrast, the periphery's strong momentum appears to be fading, though Italy saw a services-led rebound. Overall, business optimism has improved to its highest since May 2024, despite remaining low by historical standards. This trend reinforces the narrative of a two-speed economy, with domestic demand as the main engine of growth. While a moderation in services drove the headline slowdown, the sector continues to handily outperform weaker, export-oriented manufacturing, which faces global headwinds. The final manufacturing PMI was revised up to 49.5, with German firms expressing optimism for the year ahead. From a broader perspective, the data signals persistent price pressures, as input costs accelerate across both sectors and firms pass these on to clients. While the impact of GDP growth on loans to the non-financial corporate sector builds over time and takes a couple of quarters to reach its peak, the effect is more persistent (Exhibit 5). The Boost From the Hard Assets Rotation Following a 2025 metals rally, many commodities are off to a strong and volatile start in 2026 (Exhibit 1). Client conversations suggest that investor appetite to diversify into hard assets amidst macro and geopolitical uncertainty (sometimes associated with the debasement theme) is a key driver of the rally.1 Hard assets are tangible, physical items that have intrinsic value, including commodities, real estate, infrastructure and equipment, and tend to hold value over time, especially during inflation or economic uncertainty.2 Given the rotation from soft assets (e.g. fixed income or capital-light equities) to hard assets, we analyze the link between active investor positioning and prices, which is close for commodities such as oil (Exhibit 2). Specifically, how would a sustained rise in active investor positioning into commodities affect prices? And what are the risks from this rotation to the prices of gold, copper, and oil? 1 Other drivers of the rise in energy prices include the return of a geopolitical risk premium and the cold US winter. 2 The intrinsic value or payoff from holding commodities is the marginal value of benefits that inventories provide (e.g. smooth production, avoiding stockouts) net of storage and insurance costs, i.e. the marginal convenience yield. Third, the threshold for meaningful policy easing in the property market has risen for three reasons. First, if the main goal of economic restructuring is to reduce reliance on ever-rising property prices and debt-heavy construction, then the government will likely only manage the downturn, not reverse it (Exhibit 12). Second, as time goes on, the drag from the property sector will begin to fade, while gains from high-tech industries will spread, reducing the need for property easing. Third, policymakers believe their policy space is limited and should be reserved for more critical objectives and tougher periods. records.text: Using our GSFEER model we can arrive at a rough estimate of the potential currency impact—specifically to CAD’s “fair value”—from a displacement of Canada’s crude exports to the US. In a scenario where this 12-14% of Canadian crude exports are replaced by Venezuelan crude, this would result in current account deterioration of about $14bn or 0.6% of GDP . USD/CAD’s fair value under this external balance approach would rise by about 1% (from 1.36 currently). Estimates using CAD’s typical sensitivity to oil prices, such as the beta to oil prices in our CAD GSBEER model, yield similar results. We would caveat these stylized estimates in a few ways. While changes in fair value estimates are typically small, the implied impact to CAD using oil price sensitivities could be meaningfully larger in the case that US refiners struggle to absorb the extra supply and oil prices decline more than we currently expect. On the other hand, even in a scenario where Venezuela production increases more than currently expected, Canada would likely be able to reroute some of its US crude exports elsewhere. For example, it has been reported that upcoming trade agreements between Canada and China could include additional exports of Canadian crude to China. While China still accounts for only a small share of Canada’s total energy exports, volumes to China have increased dramatically since the 2024 Trans Mountain (TMX) expansion (Exhibit 7). A long week for India US President Trump and India Prime Minister Modi announced reduction in US import tariffs on India to 18% from 50%, on 2 February7 , marking a long-awaited conclusion of the India-US trade agreement. India was the only major economy within the region which had not reached a 'trade deal' with the US in 2025. Recall that the 50% tariffs on India, imposed in late August 2025, included a 25% reciprocal tariff and additional 25% for importing Russian oil. India's commerce minister later clarified8 that a joint statement by the two sides will be issued 'in the next 4-5 days' , while legal text of the first tranche of the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement will be signed by mid-March. With 18% total tariff, India is firmly back in the trade-competitiveness play, with its average US tariff now comparable with peer economies. We estimate lower tariffs will add ~30bp to headline GDP growth (essentially reversing the threat posed by 50% tariffs until now). We acknowledge that lack of confirmation by PM Modi on India's Russian oil purchases and the commitment to buy US500bn of US goods (including agriculture) weighs heavily on the eventual implementation of this deal. India has tapered its imports of crude oil from Russia in FY26 (share of total is down to 33.2% from 35.8% in FY25 after the secondary tariffs came into effect). records.text: Credit Growth Resilience in the Making: How, Where and When? Leveraging 15 years of data in the Euro area and excluding the pandemic years, we quantify the positive relationship between economic growth and bank credit growth in the Euro area. Our VAR analysis makes the intuitive assumption that GDP growth leads loan growth and allows us to study the different responses for households and the non-financial corporate sector1. In our estimates we control for changes in financial conditions and lending standards for both households and the non-financial corporate sector (Exhibit 4). 1 Our empirical analysis uses data from 2003 and drops the years of the pandemic (2020-22). We use a Cholesky ordering where GDP growth is ranked first and has contemporaneous effect on household and non financial sector loan growth. The ordering of household and non financial sector loan growth do not affect our results. records.text: Although the Census Bureau's estimates of retail sales are still running about a month behind the usual schedule following earlier shutdown-related delays, more timely indicators of consumer spending look mixed in the new year. The latest estimates from Wards showed a softening of light vehicle sales from 16.0mn in December to a soft 14.9mn saar in January (Barclays and consensus 15.2mn). Meanwhile, the latest Chicago Fed CARTS forecast—which is formed using a factor-based approach that weights credit card tabulations, retail foot traffic, sentiment, and other indicators—points to a deceleration of ex-motor vehicle retail sales to 0.1% m/m in January from 0.5% m/m increases in November and December. Our Alternative Data Signals models point to nominal increases in the control group ranging from 0.2% to 0.6% m/m in January. We think next week's official December's retail sales estimates from the Census Bureau will show some mild deceleration following November's strong readings, with the headline rising 0.4% m/m (consensus: 0.4% m/m) and the control group up 0.4% m/m (consensus: 0.4% m/m). In our view, this mild slowing would presage the deceleration of PCE from about 3.0% q/q saar in Q4 to 2.0% q/q saar in Q1, which also reflects drag from the downwardly distorted estimates of inflation during Q4's prolonged shutdown. Historically, the 2017–2018 period is a comparable reference point from the export cycle perspective. The BoK hiked twice (once a year) during that period – but the absolute level of the starting policy rate was 125bp lower. Furthermore, we think markets are factoring in the potential for inflation risk given concerns that elevated USDKRW levels could give way to a prolonged period of KRW weakness that adds to inflation through imports. This is not our base case. We remain bullish on the KRW over the medium term (see page 10) and expect USDKRW to decline this year. That said, we already held this view in light of the rise in the neutral rate and the ability of the Fed to use interest rate policy more liberally. Under current FOMC preferences, we think the Fed would only turn to asset purchases under recessionary conditions that push the policy rate to the effective lower bound. A higher threshold for liquidity interventions also means reserve management purchases, such as bill purchases used to stabilize money market functioning, would be used more sparingly and potentially at a slower cadence. Effects of Reduced Communication A central pillar of Warsh’s critique concerns the Fed’s communication strategy, which he views as overly influential in shaping market expectations. (3) The state of the Swiss economy and (domestic) inflation pressures could turn out to be weaker than expected, requiring an even more expansionary policy stance. (4) Neutral could be lower than we (and the SNB) think so that the SNB could come to the conclusion that the current policy stance is not expansionary. With prices for many industrial and precious metals having ascended in prior months to highs not seen since the post-pandemic inflation surge, our recent research considers the extent that this development risks persistently higher inflation. According to our modeling, the direct passthrough from higher base metal prices to consumer prices is rather modest. However, indirect effects through prices of inputs and other channels are potentially meaningful: a persistent 10% shock to metals prices tends to raise headline CPI by 0.3pp over two years and core CPI by about 0.2pp over the same period. records.text: M Foundation 18 What Could Trigger a Further Unwind of the JPY Carry Trade? As we discussed in USD/JPY forecast revision, January 16, 2026, principal component analysis of daily moves in G10 currencies versus USD over the past half-year shows the second principal component – which turns out to be strongly correlated with global risk sentiment – having a critical impact on the performance of USD/JPY relative to other currency pairs (see Exhibit 29 and Exhibit 30 ). Risk sentiment has of course been quite good over the period in question, which likely goes a long way towards explaining the underperformance of JPY (as a funding currency) versus classic risk currencies such as the Aussie dollar and Scandies. Moreover, we would expect use of JPY as a funding currency to have become that much more appealing following the ascent of Sanae Takaichi to the leadership amid concerns that Japan might be set to take an even more expansionary approach to fiscal policy. So, what might cause the negative risk premium priced into JPY to shrink or even disappear altogether? Other than for actual JPY-buying intervention (see below), we would basically expect this to require some sort of catalyst that serves to depress global risk sentiment and/or alleviate concerns about Japanese fiscal expansion risk. We similarly find a slight positive correlation between industry-level AI adoption and unemployment among college graduates (Exhibit 5). Since tariff revenues have become a key component of government revenues, we think the administration is keen to maintain the tariff rate near current levels. Indeed, the loss of tariff revenue could widen term premia (we estimate by as much as 20bp in the 10y for every USD100bn in annual revenue) and thereby worsen affordability vis-a-vis higher borrowing rates. The more likely possibility in our view is that the administration tweaks the composition of replacement tariffs, easing up on visible consumer goods and shifting the burden to more upstream/industrial inputs. While tariff costs could still find their way up the value chain and to consumer prices over time, in the near term it would be inflation relief for impacted consumer goods categories. However, productivity measures are notoriously volatile and it is quite difficult to disentangle structural and cyclical productivity developments in historical data, much less in real time. For this reason, the FOMC has generally been cautious and slow-moving in updating its beliefs about underlying productivity based on published data. The anecdotal evidence of AI on productivity is also mixed. On the one hand, companies across the economy have been vocal about how they are introducing AI in their workflows, allowing them to maintain or increase output at lower cost. On the other, an MIT report last year found that 95% of generative AI pilots at companies were unsuccessful. Another study found that experienced programmers were 19% slower when they used AI. The world's leading CRM company made waves when it replaced 4,000 workers with AI, only to later reportedly regret the decision as it realised it was overly confident in AI's ability. Finally, even if the US is on the cusp of a productivity revolution, it is not clear that the policy prescription is the same as it was for Greenspan, who was already seeing downward pressures on costs and inflation. In principle, the build-out phase might require higher interest rates until the productivity gains are actually realised. On Jan. 28th, Reuters again reported that Beijing has given the green light to Bytedance, BABA, and Tencent to purchase more than 400k H200 chips in total, with other firms now joining the queue for approval. However, the same media reports suggest these approvals came with conditions and they may be too restrictive, therefore these companies were not yet converting the approvals to purchase orders. This back and forth speaks to the sensitivity of the circumstances, as the Chinese government tries to balance between supporting development of domestic chip industry and giving AI labs access to higher-end chips to be competitive globally. If worse comes to worst, there is a possibility that these companies will be required to purchase mostly, if not all, domestic chips. This could mean some companies will not be able to purchase enough chips due to SMIC's 7nm production capacity constraint. While SMIC aims to significantly increase its 7nm capacity in 2026, the process will take time, and supply constraints likely will remain after the capacity expansion. If companies can secure enough Chinese chips and address system and model compatibility issues, switching from the H20 to domestic Huawei Ascend 910C chips may lower capex by ~10% in certain scenarios. Looking out to 2026, we estimate total tokens generated by these Chinese companies will grow around 117% yoy to 25,221T , mostly driven by growing adoption of chatbot apps and AI features

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 The effective tariff rate and high-frequency container traffic The tariff rate on US imports is tracking at ~11% in the November 2025 trade data The Trump administration imposed additional tariffs on trading partners as of August 7 that pushed the effective tariff rate higher to 16.0%. Since then, negotiations with three of the US's largest trading partners – Mexico, Canada, and China – continue to proceed on a separate track. In addition, Section 232 reviews on trade in semiconductors, lumber, and pharmaceuticals, among others, remain ongoing. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on the legality of IEEPA tariffs in early November and we await a potential ruling, which could come any day that the court is in session. Given the calendar for the court, the earliest date for a decision to be released will be February 20. If IEEPA tariffs are invalidated, the effective tariff rate may move lower temporarily as the administration uses other trade authority to reconstitute its tariff regime. See here for more detailed views. The US trade data in the last three months of data (Sept-Nov 2025) has shown some stabilization in trade patterns: there has been a shift in the composition of US imports, as well as in the importing countries. If these patterns remain in place, the effective tariff rate will likely stabilize around the currently observed rate of ~11%, and remain in the low- teens. With prices for many industrial and precious metals having ascended in prior months to highs not seen since the post-pandemic inflation surge, our recent research considers the extent that this development risks persistently higher inflation. According to our modeling, the direct passthrough from higher base metal prices to consumer prices is rather modest. However, indirect effects through prices of inputs and other channels are potentially meaningful: a persistent 10% shock to metals prices tends to raise headline CPI by 0.3pp over two years and core CPI by about 0.2pp over the same period. Although we have not incorporated such effects into our baseline, we think upswings of this nature could shift the distribution of inflation outcomes higher, especially if they prove durable. 6 February 2026 14 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: Productivity, please!

records.text: Older college graduates appear to have experienced a larger increase in their unemployment rate than usual mainly because the industries that disproportionately employ college graduates—such as information services, finance, and professional and business services—have reduced hiring more sharply over the past few years (Exhibit 4). Job growth in industries that employ the largest shares of college graduates averaged -9k/month over 2023-2025 (vs. +44k/month on average over 2017-2019). By contrast, job growth in the industries that employ the smallest shares of college graduates averaged +12k/month over that period (vs. +31k/month on average over 2017-2019). records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 9 Exhibit 11: Domestic investors have not purchased much super-long JGBs Source: JSDA, Morgan Stanley Research Exhibit 12: Domestic investors overall continue to ramp up their outward securities investment Source: Japan MoF, Morgan Stanley Research Why aren’t we seeing repatriation? As we discussed in 2023 Plan of Investors in Japan, May 19, 2023, different domestic (institutional) investors should have quite different motivations for investing in foreign bonds. In the context of FX, it also bears noting that it is really only investment trusts, pension funds and life insurers that will tend to meet their foreign currency procurement needs via the spot FX market. The banking sector completely separates its JPY and foreign currency balance sheets for asset management purposes, and will accordingly tend to use foreign currency funds to invest in foreign bonds and JPY funds (deposit) when investing in JGBs with no real concept of 'repatriation'. Life insurers hedge some of their foreign bond holdings against FX risk, meaning that not all of their capital flows will necessarily impact the spot market (see Exhibit 13 ). Moreover, lifers have, in any case, been reducing their exposure to both foreign bonds and domestic bonds of late while putting greater weight on outward direct investment and investment trusts (see Exhibit 14 ).

records.text: Why Has the Unemployment Rate of College Graduates Risen More Than Usual? The unemployment rate for college graduates has risen 0.7pp since January 2023 to 2.8% in December 2025, well above the 2019 average of 2.1%, and it remains much more elevated than the unemployment rates for other education levels on a standardized basis (relative to its normal level and volatility over the business cycle) (Exhibit 1). In today’s Daily, we check back in on college graduates’ labor market outcomes and revisit questions we investigated last summer: are college graduates having a hard time finding jobs, and if so, why? We take a closer look at the college graduate and non-college graduate unemployment rates by breaking out young workers who are new or relatively new to the labor force based on their age and what level of education they have completed. For both education groups, the unemployment rates for young workers (dashed lines in Exhibit 2) have risen more on a standardized basis than the unemployment rates for all other age groups (solid lines in Exhibit 2). Further, the unemployment rates for college graduates of both age groups have risen disproportionately over the past few years. Taken together, these trends suggest that the rise in the college graduate unemployment rate reflects both the impact of being a new entrant to the labor force and of being a college graduate. records.text: Global Synthesis Productivity, please! Productivity is now pivotal. How much and how fast AI will boost broad productivity growth is no longer just a matter for tech equity valuations, but will determine monetary policy, employment and debt sustainability. Next week, Japan's election, payrolls and CPI will be in focus. Productivity moves to center stage "Productivity isn't everything, but, in the long run, it is almost everything, " Paul Krugman famously stated, emphasising the critical role of productivity in driving economic growth and improving living standards. In the present, productivity certainly is almost everything, but not only in the long run, but also in the much shorter run. Many of today's equity valuations imply high future earnings from expected AI-driven productivity improvements. Notably, this week's sell-offs in some of the leading tech stocks have shown that investors seem eager to see evidence of this earnings growth sooner rather than later. Instead of embracing more announcements of record- breaking AI investments by hyperscalers, investors have grown cautious about the proportionality of capex spending vs. earnings growth. The question of companies' earnings growth from AI is ultimately one of AI's effect on productivity in the broader economy. AI not only needs to provide gains within the tech space itself, but must turn into the General Purpose Technology (GPT) that transforms an entire economy. Here also, expectations are high. records.text: This month’s report will be accompanied by the annual benchmark revision to the establishment survey and a methodological update to the birth-death model. The BLS’s preliminary estimate of the benchmark payrolls revision indicated that cumulative payroll growth between April 2024 and March 2025 would be revised 911k lower. We estimate that the final downward revision will likely be somewhat smaller—in the range of 750-900k—as job growth in the QCEW, which informs the revision, has been revised up since the BLS issued the preliminary estimate. The BLS will also update the net birth-death forecasts in the post-benchmark period (April 2025-December 2025) to incorporate information from the QCEW and the monthly payrolls survey. A downward revision to the post-benchmark period appears likely, reflecting the continued slowdown in the job growth measured by the QCEW and weak private payroll growth measured by the establishment survey during post-benchmark period. Starting with this month’s report, the birth-death model will incorporate current sample information each month. This methodological change is intended to reduce the magnitude of annual revisions, as changes in employment at continuing establishments will provide additional information about current net job creation from firm births and deaths beyond what the current methodology based on lagged QCEW data already does. records.text: Oil – soft fundamentals and Venezuelan sanctions relief: Coming into this year, we expected crude prices to fall on the back of stock builds in the Atlantic Basin, albeit with geopolitical risks providing a strong floor. The US intervention in Venezuela should add another downward influence on crude prices, as Venezuelan supply volumes increase against this backdrop of an already bearish oil market. We expect the US and Venezuelan governments to eventually negotiate a pathway for sanctions relief and the return of Venezuelan barrels to the market. A full removal of the blockage would enable a swift unwinding of current floating storage of oil, depressing prices in the near term (a couple of months). The negotiation process will likely take several months, so our updated base case assumes sanctions relief in Q2. This is why our forecast dips to USD51/bbl in June (see Global Macro: Impact of Venezuelan regime shift, dated 8 January). Gradual longer-term recovery: Looking further ahead, we see only a slow ramp- up in oil production. The country’s broader energy infrastructure (upgraders, diluent supply, power grid) is badly degraded, while a structural increase in supply would require steps from elections, debt renegotiations and multilateral loans to new production contracts, auctions and more. records.text: Spread structures look attractive to hedge the risk of a small correction and take advantage of elevated risk-off skew to reduce cost. In the near term, the supportive macro backdrop should limit the risk of large market sell-offs. Besides equity put spreads, CDS payer spreads and VIX call spreads look attractive given their high max payoff ratio compared with history (Exhibit 42). FX options are also attractive as FX realised volatility is starting to pick up again, driven by US policy uncertainty, Japan elections, and commodity prices — USD/CHF in particular has started to realised larger tails (Exhibit 43). FX options can hedge specific scenarios and look particularly attractive if the move in a risk scenario aligns with a currency’s medium-term trend. We like puts on USD/CHF as a hedge to growth and geopolitical shocks — our FX team expects continued Dollar weakness in 2026. While rates vol has lagged other assets, a rise in longer-dated rates remains a key risk for balanced portfolios with a more procyclical rotation across assets and also lingering fiscal risks. records.text: Potentially Large Price Boosts for Small Commodity Markets Investors Role in Commodity Markets There are two types of investors in commodity futures markets: “speculators” or “active” investors, including hedge funds, CTAs and swap dealers, and “index” or “passive” investors, comprised of pension funds, endowments and other real money investors. Our statistical analysis focuses on the price impact of active investors because index investors tend to have little, if any, impact on prices.3 That said, investor conversations suggest that certain passive investors (e.g. pensions funds) are increasingly considering rotating to hard assets, including commodities. To understand investors’ impact on prices of commodities—physical assets that deliver intrinsic value when consumed—consider the following linkages between physical (or spot) markets and futures markets: Convergence: as futures approach expiration, their price converges to the spot n physical price. Price discovery: futures prices reflect market expectations of future supply and n demand (with a risk premium). Hedging: futures markets allow producers/consumers in the physical market to n manage selling/purchasing price risk. Arbitrage: When the price difference between the physical and futures markets n becomes too large, arbitrageurs step in. Note that we do not expect any increase in TIPS sizes in FY27. The key risk to our view is if Treasury decides to lean on T-bills further due to the Fed’s reserve management purchases (RMPs) of T-bills and the Fed’s reinvestment of MBS prepays into T-bills. Indeed, Treasury added a new sentence stating that they are “monitoring SOMA purchases of Treasury bills and growing demand for Treasury bills from the private sector. ” However, RMPs are still small relative to T- bill issuance as we expect net positive private supply of ~$400bn this year, which means private T-bill share is still moving higher unless coupons are increased at some point. In addition, it is not clear whether Fed Chair nominee Kevin Warsh will look to reduce the SOMA portfolio and/or cease RMPs completely. Still, RMPs in the short term tilts the risk for coupon increases to come after our November 2026 base case (perhaps February 2027). On 8 Jan, it set a 2026 production target of 600 Mt, vs 740 Mt for the 2025 target and 790 Mt actual 2025 output (vs consensus expectations of 2026 target closer to 700 Mt). Given domestic supply obligations, we expect any cuts to pass through to exports. Last week's indications of stricter RKAB quotas being issued show some commitment to cuts: Initial market reaction to the new output target was limited, as the target's enforcement mechanisms - RKAB quotas, DMO - were still unclear for 2026. Last week's preliminary indications of 2026 RKAB quotas show significant cuts for smaller miners. We see downside risk to Indonesian exports that is not yet fully reflected in seaborne prices, forecasting exports to fall 17% YoY to 435 Mt. Low-cal coal grades should benefit most; however, substitution effects should lend support to higher-cal grades. We flag upside risk to our 2026 price target of $116/t. Key risks: Policy and quota relaxation if higher prices do not materialise. Given the importance of mining royalties for state budgets, exports for foreign exchange earnings, and mines for employment opportunities, the government may soften cuts if revenue upside is not forthcoming. It cited new evidence that structural changes in wage-setting will not keep adding to inflationary pressures. • Bailey and Mann, who voted to hold in Feb., expressed greater confidence that upside inflation risks would be mitigated by lower near-term path for inflation and placed greater emphasis on risks from weaker activity. Mann, who has been a hawk, is looking close to voting for cuts saying “New analysis and current developments have moved the appropriate time for cut in Bank Rate closer.” • The downgrades to inflation forecasts were fairly dovish. Inflation is notably lower than expected in November partly on the back of disinflationary Budget measures. The BoE expects 2026 Q2 inflation at 2.1% (vs. 2.9% before), 2027 Q1 at 1.7% (vs. 2.2% before), 2028 Q1 at 1.8% (vs. 2.1% before) and 2029 Q1 at 2.0%. Hiromu Uezato hiromu.uezato@morganstanleymufg.com +81 3 6836-8428 Linking the JPY carry trade to JPY weakness Recent price action suggests that JPY’s usual cause-and-effect relationship has inverted, with a weaker JPY and higher JGB yields simultaneously. Traditionally, one would expect JPY to strengthen as interest rate differentials between overseas markets and Japan narrow via capital flow. So far, capital flow data have offered only limited evidence that domestic investors are rotating meaningfully back into JGBs, even as their yields have become more attractive on a relative basis. Investment trusts continue to export capital, reflecting households’ demand for hedges against both inflation and JPY depreciation. records.text: M Global Idea 2 Meaningful further reduction of bank reserves runs into banks’ demand for reserves because of things like the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and by banks’ internal liquidity policies. So a material reduction could tighten liquidity conditions in funding markets, as the Fed goes from “ample” reserves toward “scarce” reserves. The fed funds and repo rates could become volatile, but also move above IORB under the existing floor system. To prevent excessive volatility as reserve supply and demand fluctuate around month-ends, Treasury settlements, tax dates, or money fund rebalancing—the Fed would likely rely more on temporary OMOs to add liquidity as needed. The Fed could also lower the rate it pays on reserves and in the RRP facility. The hope would be that over time the pressure in markets would lead to lower demand for reserves, as well. Prior to the Financial Crisis, the Fed intervened daily in markets to try to hit the target federal funds rate. A technical option exists to shrink the Fed balance sheet without shrinking reserves. If greater coordination with Treasury develops, the Treasury could reduce its Treasury General Account (TGA) at the Fed, for example from almost $1trn down to $500bn, allowing the Fed to reduce its holdings of Treasury securities by $500bn. The Fed’s balance sheet would be smaller, reserves would not need to change in that scenario, and the Treasury’s interest payments to the Fed would be lower. The turn-of-the-year print will also feature the 2026 seasonal adjustment factors, revisions to historical factors extending back through 2021, and updated relative importance weights. As discussed in detail in our preview, we expect the latest annual seasonal adjustment factors to show, at most, a 4-5bp shift in m/m inflation, in either direction, in any given month. The updated relative importance weights— which fold in information from the recently released 2024 consumer expenditure survey— should show only modest changes, on balance. This would include a modest boost to weights on housing rents and used cars, balanced mostly by a somewhat lower weight on new cars. We expect January's CPI estimates to translate to a 0.37% m/m increase in core PCE price inflation, which would come on the heels of a December increase that looks to be about 0.40% m/m given the PPI and CPI estimates on hand through December. records.text: After having declined almost continuously since its peak in 2017/18, German n industrial production (IP) looks to have bottomed last year and recently manufacturing orders have ticked up notably. That said, the dataflow remains highly volatile, as exemplified by a weak December IP reading, and the several manufacturing indicators available—including IP , orders, sales, and surveys— send diverging signals. In this Analyst we proceed in three steps to extract a signal on underlying dynamics from the volatile dataflow. First, we investigate the relevance of various indicators for near-term forecasting n of IP , the most prominent manufacturing activity indicator. We find that the ifo survey contains more information for projecting month-ahead IP growth than the PMI. That said, hard data that progressively becomes available ahead of the IP release, in particular truck toll-mileage and manufacturing sales, significantly improve on the near-term forecast. Our model currently predicts a rebound in January IP following a weak December. Second, we develop a framework for extracting the underlying signal for German n manufacturing activity, which we leverage for medium-term forecasting. Our statistical (“dynamic factor”) model maps granular data on surveys and growth in sales, orders, and IP into sector-specific trends and common underlying factors. records.text: M Idea 4 • The proposed production cut would predominantly affect exports if it materialises, as supply to the domestic market is protected via the DMO. We expect the DMO to remain broadly stable YoY at ~255 Mt, as domestic coal power demand is flat- to-rising. Actual Indonesian coal production stood at 790 Mt in 2025, exceeding the 2025 government target by ~7%. If production were to fall from this level to the new target in 2026, that would imply 24% downside, or an almost 200 Mt output cut. Assuming the DMO is stable YoY at 255 Mt, then that would leave 345 Mt of thermal coal to be exported to the global market. That would imply a ~180 Mt YoY cut to Indonesia exports. The global export market is just over ~1 billion tonnes, suggesting a 16% cut to global seaborne traded supply. A cut of this size would be very significant for the thermal coal market, but ultimately prices did not react very strongly to this news. A wait-and-see approach was adopted instead, with market participants waiting for the release of the RKAB quotas and DMO to gauge how strongly the government would be enforcing its new target. Given the volume of RKAB quotas approved usually exceeds the production target, it seems likely that the maximum permitted level of production would not fall as low as 600 Mt, reducing the magnitude of output cuts and muting initial price reaction. records.text: 10 Questions for multi-asset investors early in 2026 (1) How did multi-asset portfolios and funds perform in 2025? A global multi-asset portfolio performed strongly in USD in 2025 despite the Liberation day drawdown, but regional performance differed materially, with European multi-asset funds lagging. Our proxy for the World Portfolio (GSMBWP01), which tracks the majority of global financial assets including private markets and crypto (currently roughly US$280trn), delivered a return close to 20% in USD. Based on comparable history of a world portfolio proxy of just equities, bonds and Gold since 1950, this is the 90th percentile and follows two years of already strong performance — the 3-year rolling annualised return is 14% at the end of 2025 (Exhibit 2, 90th percentile since 1950). This was mainly due to another strong year for equities even though leadership shifted from US to EM equities — but most risky assets had a strong year and commodities, especially Gold, performed very strongly. In local returns, simple 60/40 portfolios delivered similar returns across regions (Exhibit 3) but a risk parity strategy would have materially outperformed in the US (Exhibit 4). While rising European and Japanese 10-year bond yields created some drag in multi-asset portfolios, falling US 10-year yields were a tailwind in 2025. We promised a more detailed discussion when we changed the ECB call after this week’s ECB meeting conference, here it comes. Growth: more of a “sugar rush” than a proper structural change Our Euro area growth forecasts move to 1.2% in 2026 (+20bp) and 1.3% in 2027 (-10bp). Beyond marking to market 4Q data across countries, these changes reflect a reassessment of the impact of the German fiscal package on the economy. We now think this will be more of a “sugar rush” scenario for growth. Indeed, our forecasts for Germany move from 0.7% and 1.6% in 2026 and 2027, to 1.0% and 1.7% respectively, but sequential growth looks very different. It goes from 0 over the past six years to 2.5% qoq saar in 2H26E before slowing to just below 1% by 2H27E. Why? The composition of higher fiscal spending after last year’s fiscal reforms is directed more towards “consumption” than proper investment, eventually leading to bigger growth effects in the short terms, but fewer medium-term gains. Germany is a lot less likely to be able to sustain strong growth beyond the next two years. And complementary structural reform to bolster medium-term growth potential also looks tough to deliver. Defence is relatively better designed (showing also in factory orders) and this is largely why we could see growth closer to 1% than zero

records.text: M Idea 4 Reducing the consumption tax rate for foods from 8% to zero for two years as proposed by the LDP would mean forgoing around JPY 5 trillion/year in revenues. The ruling party has indicated that it would look to plug this gap by reviewing various subsidies and tax breaks. Our view is that even without such policy changes it should still be possible to avoid an increase in market issuance of JGBs by depleting the available reserves of front-loaded refunding bond issuance. However, it needs to be acknowledged that there might be a high political hurdle to raising the food consumption tax rate back to 8% after two years have elapsed. The CRA would need to find a more lasting fiscal solution if looking to grant foods a permanent consumption tax exemption. It cites investment income from a sovereign wealth fund (SWF), but the SWF itself exists only at the conceptual stage within Komeito and has no concrete funding vehicle. It remains unclear what funding sources would accompany the CRA’s call for an early tax rate cut. That said, since the CRA advocates securing funding without relying on deficit-financing bonds, excessive concerns over an increase in market issuance are likely unwarranted. To summarize, neither the ruling coalition nor the largest opposition party currently appears to favour increasing JGB issuance for the purpose of funding the consumption tax cut. Extracting the Underlying Signal from a Volatile Dataset Looking beyond the nowcasting of near-term IP growth, the identification of a common underlying signal from the various monthly data remains quite challenging. First, monthly growth rates of IP in the manufacturing sector—the most important hard indicator for manufacturing—are negatively autocorrelated (Exhibit 5, left). A month with above-average growth is typically followed by a month with below-average growth, and vice versa. This stands in contrast to other high profile monthly data and makes it hard to separate the signal on underlying industry dynamics from the noise. While moving averages of the growth rate are less volatile and smooth out the monthly noise, they complicate timely identification of turning points. Second, the signal from different data points—some of which are generally thought to be more forward-looking than IP growth—can diverge (Exhibit 5, right). We continue to like a combination of regional and style diversification, selective commodity exposure, as well as more allocations to alternatives such as hedge funds, private markets and alternative risk premia. Diversification in broad multi-asset portfolios has improved materially since 2022, in particular across asset classes (Exhibit 30). Diversification between equities and bonds has improved and there has been more benefit from commodity allocations, especially Gold. Similarly, international diversification benefits picked up, with more cycle and policy divergence — this has been the case in both bonds and equities. Larger allocations to smaller assets and alternatives should help enhance diversification of benchmarked equity/bond portfolios in 2026. Defensive indices have helped buffer YTD volatility after having materially de-rated in recent years — especially during the sharp Software sell-off due to AI disruption fears, both the S&P 500 low volatility Index and the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats Index outperformed materially (Exhibit 31). The same has been true for the DJB Global Infrastructure Index, which is more capital-heavy and less exposed to AI disruption. Those indices tend to outperform in ‘risk off’ episodes, especially when driven by the tech sector, but tend to have similar risk-adjusted returns to equity benchmarks over the long-run — we like risk-neutral, levered exposure to such defensive styles. Next week's data deluge brings crucial payrolls and CPI However, in the very near term, the incoming labour market and inflation data will be more important. This week, number of indicators suggested that the job market ran on the soft side in January relative to expectations. Initial jobless claims jumped from 212k to 231k in seasonally adjusted terms, returning to levels of a few months ago, though cold weather likely affected the print. Revelio Labs estimated a decline in NFP employment of 13k in January, compared with c. +30k in Nov/Dec, broadly consistent with the soft January private job gain (22k) reported by ADP . Perhaps most significantly, job openings in the December JOL TS survey moved down notably for the third consecutive month, to 6.5mn, indicating downside risks to labour demand conditions (or already reflecting the positive productivity shock?). All this increases the importance of next week's rescheduled January employment report. We forecast a +50k gain in headline and private nonfarm employment, alongside a 0.1pp decline in the unemployment rate, to 4.3%. After this week's data, we see downside risks to this forecast. records.text: Lesson #5: Higher US tariffs moderated Chinese export growth The biggest surprise of 2025 was the resilience of Chinese exports. Despite higher US tariffs, Chinese export volume increased by more than 8% in 2025. However, monthly data indicates that US tariffs did impact Chinese exports. Exhibit 9 shows export volumes dropped in April and May when US-China trade tensions escalated, remaining below the 2023Q2–2024Q3 trend through October. After the Trump-Xi meeting in South Korea at the end of October—when the US partially rolled back tariffs on China— export volume rose notably in November and December. This pattern suggests that while rerouting and redirecting helped offset much of the negative impact of US tariffs on Chinese exports, the effect was not fully neutralized. If Chinese exports grew by more than 8% despite the drag from higher US tariffs, the underlying trend could be stronger than 8% per year. Should the US further cut tariffs on China in April during President Trump’s planned visit, Chinese exports could rise again, similar to the increases seen last November and December. Meanwhile, the "divided Diet" structure, in which the ruling coalition lacks a majority, will continue in the House of Councillors (the Upper House). Although the ability to override the Upper House's decisions with a two-thirds majority in the Lower House diminishes the Upper House's influence on bill passage, any approach that overtly disregards the Upper House could provoke public criticism. How the Takaichi administration engages with the Upper House will remain a crucial point in assessing its political stability. In particular, appointments requiring Diet consent, such as the successor to the BOJ policy board member whose term expires at the end of March, need approval from both houses. The approval process will be closely watched as a rare opportunity for the Upper House to assert its presence. Additionally, the possibility remains that the ruling coalition will seek to cooperate with opposition parties to ensure smooth parliamentary proceedings in the Upper House. In such a case, the DPP would likely be the key, given the similarity of their policy stances. The Foreign Exchange Flow Indicator (FXFI) is a measure of the currency flows of institutional investors. It is designed to gauge institutional investor sentiment toward a set of developed and emerging markets currencies. It is also possible that the extent of overvaluation and the drag that it implies on forward returns is overstated—the valuation metric that we use here (the cyclically-adjusted Shiller P/E ratio) relies on the past 10 years of earnings. If the productivity possibilities of AI are leading investors to price higher future earnings up front, before that earnings growth is realized, current valuations based on past earnings could overstate equity “richness.” AI optimism has undoubtedly been a pillar of the strong equity returns that the US has posted over the last couple of years, and we think that optimism is likely to continue. But it is also true that the market has built in significant benefits from AI into equity prices already. The tension between valuations and the cycle could grow if our baseline outlook is correct, and high valuations underscore that the downside tail could be fatter than usual if recession risk were to return more meaningfully. In the late 1990s, we saw equity volatility pick up even as stocks kept rising, as higher volatility and credit spreads signaled increased risk premium even as stocks kept rising (Exhibit 4). As we anticipated, the policy signal was for a cut as early as March - the 5:4 vote split, the forecasts, the press conference. The BoE's framework is shifting, as there is more confidence that the economy is leaving the recent period of supply-side shocks with its inflationary process largely intact. We continue to look for cuts in March, July and November. We retain our SFIZ6/Z7 flattener. The headlines: The consensus looked for a 7:2 vote for a hold, while we expected a 6:3 split, with risks of a 5:4 tally. 4 members voted for a cut today (Breeden, Ramsden, Dhingra and Taylor), while Governor Bailey and external member Mann highlighted that they are ready to reduce restrictiveness further as more evidence of disinflation trickles in. The messaging was only marginally changed - the reference to the "gradual" pace of easing was removed, and the key guidance was simple: "On the basis of the current evidence, Bank Rate is likely to be reduced further". records.text: Global Macro Strategy - Views and Trade Ideas 06 February 2026 Citi Research 8 Credit hedges may also be useful. We have stressed for some time that the risk reward for credit is worse than for equities. While this is not necessarily the case when the main issue is a rerating of the tech mega caps on AI worries, we would note that the AI disruption theme that has led to selling pressure on the software names has also spilled into private credit. While the correlation between private credit and public credit is not airtight, there is some alpha from using private credit related equities (in the form of business development companies) to trade US public credit. In particular, if our private credit equity proxy (shown in Figure 16) is trading below the 55dma, which is currently the case, there is some slight alpha by shorting credit. While the results are largely driven by 2015/2016 and 2020, it is noteworthy that the unconditional active information ratio improves from 0.51 to 2.1 for the case when private credit equities trade above the 55dma. We therefore stick to our credit hedges, where we bought a payer spread on the US IG CDX, partly financed by selling a receiver spread. Figure 16. Private credit under pressure Figure 17. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 06 February 2026 13 That said, it is unclear how big security and defence industries can grow in total. In 2022, they accounted for c 1.3% of total output in 2022, but what is the end-point? That will largely depend on how much of the domestic defence spending will “stay at home” and how much growth via exports can be generated. Within EU-cooperation may play a big role in that. In the current geopolitical context, it strikes us as hard for German defence industry to replicate what German autos were in the distant past. What does all of this mean for public finance trajectories? . The German public deficit ended 2025 at 2.4% of GDP, much lower than the 3.25% for 2025 in the draft budget plan sent to Brussels last fall. Part of that may be due to implementation delays from late 2025 budget approvals. Given our discussion above, we would assume the budget to widen by c 1.5% of GDP this year to 3.9% and further in 2027 on further increases in defence. Needless to say that if our growth scenario is right, German public finance dynamics would change for the foreseeable future. As per our analysis last spring, deficit correction well below the 3% could be difficult in the medium term; the debt ratio would move on a firm upward trend (Exhibit 14). The gap to other Euro area members would remain large for a while, but narrow (perhaps with the exception of France). records.text: nsumption rather than investment components with higher immediate fiscal multipliers, but very low medium-term growth effects. Scope for growth enhancing reforms is limited, too The relocating of investment spending from the regular budget in the SVIK is symptomatic of severe political capital constraints to deliver structural reform and optimize spending. Last year’s pension reform (extending the 48% replacement ratio until 2031) or the heated discussion around a proposal to eliminate the statutory right of employees to part time (introduced as part of the 2002-05 labour market reforms to facilitate spreading insufficient work across larger number of people) are symptomatic. A glass half-full view would suggest reforms are easier to implement when the economy is doing well, or at least growing again. So perhaps we just need to wait a little longer. The glass half empty view would be that Germany’s pre-Covid track record on reform when growth is ok is rather underwhelming. And generally, reforms tend to be easier at the start of political mandates, before the political economy complicates. But perhaps the very big throw of the current government was exactly the fiscal reform delivered under old parliamentary composition last year; At this stage, political capital seems to run very thin, and delivering the required majorities could become increasingly complex. For more on our assessment of the MPC and its decision, see Delivering a dovish hold, 5 February 2026. MPC forecasts now broadly in line with our own The MPC revised the outlook for real GDP lower when compared to the forecast it released in November. This was in part due to the data outturns being weaker, but also slower quarterly growth expected in 2026. The MPC now expects annual average growth in 2026 to be 0.9% (-0.3pp), 2027 to be 1.5% (-0.1pp) and 2028 to be 1.9% (+0.1pp). This compares to our own forecasts for 2026 and 2027 of 1.3% and 1.8%, respectively. Australia: Fiscal pulse – Cyclical strength vs structural slippage Fiscal policy settings remain expansionary, even as public demand growth cooled in 2025 and GDP growth was increasingly driven by private demand. We estimate a positive fiscal impulse will provide a growth tailwind in 2025-26, with the structural deficit declining by 0.9ppt of GDP and public demand growth re-accelerating modestly through 2026. records.text: Lessons Learned from the Last Year As the Year of the Snake ends and the Year of the Horse approaches, we reflect on key insights gained about the Chinese economy and policymaking over the past year. We share several lessons drawn from closely monitoring Chinese data and policy, and discuss their implications for 2026. Lesson #1: Mind the data quality gap (again) The quality of Chinese macroeconomic data has long been a concern for China watchers. Over the years, we have developed various proprietary indicators and written extensively on this topic (see the third edition of our “Understanding China’s Economic Statistics” and our China Data Insight series). In 2025, we observed new patterns in the official data that suggest quality issues have increased compared to recent years. For instance, the NBS Manufacturing PMI consistently rose in quarter-end months— March, June, September and December—only to drop in the following month (Exhibit 1). This pattern may reflect pressure to boost GDP growth figures toward the end of each quarter. Another example is the fixed asset investment (FAI) data. In the second half of 2025, year-over-year FAI growth posted double-digit declines. Upon closer review, we believe these sharp drops in the FAI series likely represent a statistical correction rather than a true sharp downturn in investment. We think the evidence so far is not conclusive, particularly as we note that the dispersion of compensations growth rates across sectors is rather lower, not higher, than usual. So we think that a not too strong business cycle will ultimately imply that the drift (and compensations growth) goes down too. How do we gain more conviction here? First, we will keep an eye on 4Q25 employment, due on 13 Feb. Then 4Q25 negotiated wages will be released on 20 Feb, a couple of days before 4Q25 compensations (6 March). But softening wages might only materialize in 1Q26 when many contracts are updated. 1Q26 negotiated wages will be out on 20 May and 1Q26 compensations on 5 June. Before that, we will be attentive to negotiated wages in Germany for Jan-26 and Feb-26, due around 20 March and 20 April, respectively. Let’s conclude here: what we see in the labour market closes the circle to our inflation outlook and the ECB. Wage growth will slow down further, core inflation will very likely fall from here, below that ECB target. Paired with soft growth, this creates space for more ECB rate cuts and underlies our ECB call for two more cuts this year.

records.text: 2 US Economic Weekly | 06 February 2026 2026 labor outlook: five sectors to watch Shruti Mishra BofAS • Yesterday’s labor data were soft, but the weakness was narrow and driven by one-offs such as weather and year-end restructuring/normalization from post- pandemic over-hiring. • In 2026, we think tighter immigration will keep job growth soft, even as demand firms on easing trade uncertainty and fiscal stimulus. • Within sectors, we are positive on education & health, construction and trade & transport, negative on professional & business services (AI adoption), and neutral on leisure & hospitality. Time to hit the panic button on labor?… Not quite. We received a wave of labor-market data yesterday, including Challenger, Gray & Christmas layoff announcements, initial jobless claims, and JOLTS job openings, all of which were dovish on balance and raised concerns about labor market deterioration. However, it is important to place these developments in context. Jan layoffs announcements from Challenger were narrowly driven by the technology and transportation sectors, likely reflecting year end restructuring and a normalization after post-pandemic over-hiring at firms such as Amazon and UPS. This figure also came in below the one-off spike observed last Oct, driven by similar high profile job cut announcements. Infrastructure spending seems also to be increasing, but this is likely to happen at a slower pace: since the election of the new government, the sub- component of the German construction PMIs tracking civil engineering activity increased but in a volatile way and, after jumping in December, slightly declined in January. PMIs show no sign of a pick-up at the start of 2026 Incoming high-frequency indicators for January do not suggest a firming in momentum at the start of 2026. This week, January PMIs were revised lower at the EA composite level (–0.2pt to 51.3, from 51.5 in December), implying that activity entered the year roughly 1pt below its Q4 average. Sector-wise, the downward revision was driven by the services sector (–0.3pt to 51.6, 52.4 in December), while manufacturing output was revised higher (+0.2pt to 50.5, from 48.9 in December). Geographically, the composite PMI was revised down in Germany (–0.4pt to 52.1, 51.3 in December) but up in France (+0.4pt to 49.1, 50.0 in December). As referenced in The market turbulence and carry trade unwind of August 2024, Matteo Aquilina, Marco Lombardi, Andreas Schrimpf and Vladyslav Sushkoa, August 27, 2024, a better (albeit still rough) overall picture of JPY carry positions can be obtained through use of lagging indicators including the Bank of International Settlement’s IBS (International Banking Statistics) as well as over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives data. The IBS numbers offer insight into bank lending in JPY to non-Japanese non-bank financial institutions, with many such entities likely to be located in (say) the UK or the Cayman Islands and engaged in lending to hedge funds. However, we should stress that not all such loaned JPY will necessarily be channeled into carry positions. Meanwhile, OTC derivatives data tell us about unsettled FX swap, forward and currency swap positions (with JPY on one side) for banks as well as non-bank financial institutions. A particularly big increase in such positions was seen from 2020 through 2024, with non- bank financial institutions building up their exposure via FX swaps/forwards (see Exhibit 26 ).

The academic evidence is mixed. Some early case studies (often anchored on localized shocks in tight, high- demand metros) found large effects, but those results are sensitive to city-specific dynamics. Broader cross-city works that control for local characteristics typically have found effects that are smaller but still non-trivial. These are often on the order of ~0.3-0.4pp on rents for a 1pp change in immigration, rather than the 1:1 magnitudes sometimes implied in the micro studies. We also note that the large immigration increases during 2022-24 did not discernably slow rent disinflation, though it’s possible the counterfactual could be a faster decline. records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 06 February 2026 Weekly view “We are in a good place”, but where will we be next? Our conclusion first: we have taken out the ECB insurance cut, long expected in March 2026. And we added two proper cuts (25bp) in March and June 2027 in our ECB review yesterday after the press conference. To be clear, it wasn’t ECB communication that did the trick. It was uneventful, as expected. The message was one of data-dependence, no pre-commitment, a meeting- by-meeting approach from a central bank still being “in a good place”. Conviction in the March-26 cut was suffering for a few weeks, and concerns over what could happen in 2027 were growing. So it was a blend of three ECB related convictions and a re-assessment of the German fiscal trajectory, in particular. Three ECB convictions to start with… To be more precise, we hold three convictions on the ECB. First, hikes are very unlikely absent a shock in the next two years. Second, the ECB is more likely to cut than not, given the asymmetry of risks we see on both growth and inflation. Third, an insurance cut to finalise the cutting cycle would have made sense now. But that window is closing. So when/if they move, we think they will need to move more than once. records.text: We reflect on the macro data and policies we have followed closely over the past year and draw five lessons in this note. First, data quality issues in some official series have become more significant, as n seen in the quarter-end pattern of the NBS Manufacturing PMI and the double-digit declines in fixed asset investment (FAI). Second, the divergence across indicators and sectors in the Chinese economy has n grown more pronounced, with export value rising 6.6% yoy while property FAI dropped 37% yoy in December. We believe this is a result of policy design, and it is likely to persist. Third, the government’s push for technology and innovation is yielding results, n while the drag from the property market on the economy may have peaked. Fourth, policymakers have been conservative in implementing fiscal stimulus to n offset weak private demand. We think this conservative stance is linked to the elevated government debt-to-GDP ratio and heightened geopolitical uncertainties. Fifth, we find that high US tariffs did moderate China’s export growth from April n through October last year despite the fact that overall Chinese real exports increased by more than 8% in 2025. These five lessons from the past year have four implications for investors this year. First, investors should examine data carefully and comprehensively to get an n accurate picture of the Chinese economy. But upon moving into H2 2026 (particularly Q4), a wedge opens between market pricing and our forecast. The market is priced for a mid-2% glide into year end, while we see a firmer late-year profile coming in ~0.3pp (y/y) above current fixings on average in Q4. What is notable is that the inflation curve – seen through CPI swaps – has started to price in a more “normal” path for inflation baseline and inflation risk premium. Figure 34 shows that markets now expect headline CPI inflation to move lower, closer to the Fed’s target from the current 2.7% to an average of around 2.6% in the next year, and hover around 2.5% over the next few years. Contrast that with the deeply inverted inflation swap curve seen right after Liberation Day in April 2025, where markets expected tariff pass-through for the next 1-2 years before a normalization. As we have noted in this publication, delayed tariff-pass through seems likely, and there will probably be stickiness in some components of core services inflation. This view runs contrary to markets baking in near-flat pricing for inflation in the coming years. In other words, the CPI swap curve should be flatter. However, the CDS beta for the 10y ASW is positive in our specification, which is counterintuitive and may reflect collinearity with other macro/risk variables, regime effects, or the fact that CDS is an imperfect proxy for long-horizon fiscal risk. Exhibit 9 shows 30y ASW versus 5y CDS.
