Foreign Headwinds, Domestic Tailwinds Fuelled by Fiscal Spending We now take a closer look at different forces shaping manufacturing dynamics. Over the past years two important manufacturing subsectors—vehicles & parts and the energy-intensive sector, which each account for more than 15% of production (Exhibit 10, left)—have been hit by negative shocks. Between 2017 and 2021 the vehicles industry was hit by a slowdown in global demand exacerbated by Germany-specific supply constraints likely connected to stricter emissions standards. Energy-intensive industries were hit significantly by the surge in energy prices following the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine. More generally, declining international competitiveness and tariffs are weighing on the German manufacturing sector, which makes more than half of its revenues abroad and about a quarter outside of the EU (Exhibit 10, right). records.text: f Japan's (BOJ) monetary policy management. n An opportunity for normalization: Political stability can be seen as creating an environment where the BOJ can proceed with monetary policy normalization according to economic and inflation conditions with relatively less concern about political pressure. We maintain our view that the next rate hike will be in April. n Pressure for debt monetization and its side effects: On the other hand, an expansionary fiscal policy inevitably involves additional issuance of government bonds, creating an incentive for the government to curb rises in long-term interest rates. This becomes a source of pressure on the BOJ to continue its monetary easing, i.e., "pressure for debt monetization." However, this option comes with the significant side effect of triggering yen depreciation due to concerns over fiscal discipline, making it a difficult path to take. In a worst-case scenario, the government and the BOJ could be forced to intervene on two fronts—in the JGB market and the foreign exchange market—which is not a zero-probability risk. This would signify an increased degree of government control over the markets. Furthermore, with the path to a long-term administration now open, the increased likelihood that Takaichi will begin to consider the successor to BOJ Governor Ueda, whose term expires in April 2028, is also an important factor for the medium- to long-term monetary policy outlook. With GDP growth continuing to sharply exceed expectations, we think the CBC will find it harder to find reasons to cut rates. We see risks as tilted towards a rate hike in H2 2026. In our view, the CBC has so far downplayed the possibility of rate hikes – as hinted at by CPI inflation forecasts that we consider somewhat modest. In its December update, the CBC revised lower its headline 2026 CPI inflation forecast to 1.63% (from 1.66%, previously) despite significantly upgrading 2026 GDP growth. A scenario where inflation turns out to be stronger than expected, combined with growth momentum spilling over to domestic demand, could potentially trigger a rate hike from the CBC, in our view. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 markets. Hence, any real reduction in the Fed's balance sheet can only happen alongside a reduction in bank demand for reserves. Doing so may require changes to the regulatory and supervisory framework. Reserve demand is elevated, in part, due to post 2008 liquidity regulations – particularly the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Internal Liquidity Stress Test (ILST). Reforms could include permitting more flexibility in ILST assumptions, expanding the definition of Level 1 HQLA, or incorporating pre positioned discount window collateral as an eligible liquidity source. We take no view on these possibilities other than to state the obvious: regulatory reform always comes with trade offs. Altering liquidity requirements may reduce demand for reserves and permit a smaller Fed balance sheet, but reduced liquidity buffers could impair financial system resilience in periods of stress. There is no free lunch. We promised a more detailed discussion when we changed the ECB call after this week’s ECB meeting conference, here it comes. Growth: more of a “sugar rush” than a proper structural change Our Euro area growth forecasts move to 1.2% in 2026 (+20bp) and 1.3% in 2027 (- 10bp). Beyond marking to market 4Q data across countries, these changes reflect a reassessment of the impact of the German fiscal package on the economy. We now think this will be more of a “sugar rush” scenario for growth. Indeed, our forecasts for Germany move from 0.7% and 1.6% in 2026 and 2027, to 1.0% and 1.7% respectively, but sequential growth looks very different. It goes from 0 over the past six years to 2.5% qoq saar in 2H26E before slowing to just below 1% by 2H27E. Why? The composition of higher fiscal spending after last year’s fiscal reforms is directed more towards “consumption” than proper investment, eventually leading to bigger growth effects in the short terms, but fewer medium-term gains. Germany is a lot less likely to be able to sustain strong growth beyond the next two years. And complementary structural reform to bolster medium-term growth potential also looks tough to deliver. As discussed in detail in our preview, we expect the latest annual seasonal adjustment factors to show, at most, a 4-5bp shift in m/m inflation, in either direction, in any given month. The updated relative importance weights— which fold in information from the recently released 2024 consumer expenditure survey— should show only modest changes, on balance. records.text: to be slow, with plenty of trade-offs that need to be considered, and market implications that may be underappreciated There are two key ways the Fed might shrink its balance sheet from here: passive runoff—that is, allowing securities to mature without reinvestment—and active sales in the secondary market. Passive QT has done most of the heavy lifting so far, and we strongly suspect they would continue to do so if the Fed goes down this path. Since 2022, the Fed has reduced assets by over $2tn by letting Treasuries and MBS roll off. On the liability side of the balance sheet, the overnight reverse repo facility has effectively been drained, and bank reserves have been the other source of contraction. Further balance sheet shrinkage will increasingly translate into lower reserves. MBS holdings continue to fall and are being replaced with Treasuries. At the current pace, it would take close to a decade to halve the remaining portfolio. Accelerating the process would require either a sharp decline in mortgage rates or active MBS sales. We do not see the former as likely, and the latter would mean selling seasoned MBS into the current market, almost certainly widening spreads and worsening housing affordability. We see the bar for active MBS sales as very high. Exhibit 1: In the passive run-off from the Fed's balance sheet, the overnight reverse repo facility has been effectively drained. records.text: Historically, very low RAI levels were a good contrarian signal: from levels near -2 the hit ratio for positive S&P 500 returns in the subsequent 6-12 months has been very high. However, while it was a good idea to be bullish when everyone was bearish, the reverse was not necessarily true. First, there have been only 6 instances when the RAI rose above 1 since 1991, making it more difficult to extrapolate historical patterns. And in most episodes equities still delivered positive returns afterwards, even though returns slowed after about 6 months (Exhibit 9). ‘Risk off’ episodes are usually sharp and negative macro shocks are often short and trigger policy responses, and thus reversals; on the flip side, positive macro conditions that make investors bullish can linger for longer. More recently, risk appetite has been supported by growth optimism (RAI PC1) owing to a strong US macro backdrop, boosted by the Trump Administration’s ‘Big Beautiful Bill’, and also bearish views on the Dollar (RAI PC3) (Exhibit 10). As long as the macro conditions that led investors to be bullish remain in place, they can continue to support elevated risk appetite — but there is risk of reversals for the strongest procyclical rotations. Data this week confirmed that and, hence, we take out the ECB cut in March-26. But the easing bias remains and in an explicit way. We now expect the ECB to cut policy rates in March and June 2027. Why that call? We have three strong convictions from here: 1. The ECB is more likely than not to cut; that comes from the asymmetry of risks we see for both growth and inflation. 2. We still think hikes are very unlikely, absent a shock, in the next two years. 3. One cut would make sense if delivered now, as a continuation of the cutting cycle. If the ECB doesn’t cut in the next few meetings there is no room for “insurance cuts” i.e. one and done. records.text: Lesson #4: Policymakers’ conservative mindset The Chinese economy has faced significant growth headwinds in recent years. In this environment, fiscal easing would have been more effective than monetary policy to offset weak private demand. However, the Chinese government has been reluctant to loosen fiscal policy, and the large stimulus many investors expected never materialized. This lack of major fiscal stimulus likely reflects policymakers’ concerns about the elevated and rising government debt-to-GDP ratio (Exhibit 7). Ironically, relatively conservative fiscal policies may have worsened weak domestic demand, leading to deflationary pressures, lower nominal GDP growth, and a higher government debt-to-GDP ratio. For instance, China’s nominal GDP grew by only 4% in 2025, while the augmented fiscal deficit was estimated at 11% of GDP to meet the “around 5%” growth target. Japan’s experience suggests that there are other approaches to reducing the government debt-to-GDP ratio. Abenomics, which consisted of aggressive monetary easing, fiscal stimulus, and structural reforms—combined with global price increases during the COVID pandemic—led to higher inflation and nominal growth. Higher inflation and nominal growth, in turn, allowed for a lower primary deficit. Japan’s government debt-to-GDP ratio has fallen from 259% in 2020 to 216% in 2025, and our Japan economics team projects it to decline to 180% by 2035 (Exhibit 8). records.text: Germany and Europe have lost competitiveness vis-à-vis China in particular. Our China economists expect a continued increase in Chinese net exports and we consequently downgraded our growth outlook for Europe and Germany last November. Looking across German industries we find evidence for a sustained drag from Chinese competition. Industries with high exposure to Chinese export competition—measured by the increase in China’s global market share—experienced a stronger decline in industrial production over recent years (Exhibit 11, left). Compared to 2018, industries in the top fifth of China exposure—such as motor vehicles, batteries and special purpose machinery—lost more than 20% of production vs. only 5% for industries in the bottom fifth (Exhibit 11, right). While the gap opened particularly during the Covid pandemic, there has been no catch-up afterwards, which suggests that competition from China derailed a rebound in German manufacturing. We expect continued underperformance of the industries most exposed to Chinese competition. However, these unrealized gains cannot be transferred to the Japanese government budget without converting the foreign currency-denominated assets into yen. This would require either (1) selling the foreign currency assets and converting them to yen, or (2) having the FEF Special Account borrow ¥10 tn (by issuing Financing Bills) to procure the yen. It will be less extreme than in recent history, in our view, with more frequent corrections given positioning dynamics. While fundamentals, seasonality and the rates outlook remain supportive, the slowing pace in money supply, in addition to the expected boost in growth, particularly in Europe, could favour some broadening of the rally. Value would therefore be a good hedge for momentum in 2026, in our view. Hence, we think having a momentum and value blend is the best way to position this year, and it may help in periods of sharp momentum drawdowns. We had previously counted on more infrastructure-intense spending increases, with multipliers growing over time. That doesn’t seem to be the case as much as we thought, hence the earlier growth spurt, and fast fading thereafter. Broader definitions of defence and investment spending have created the risk of more consumption than investment spending. Relocating investment efforts from the regular budget into the SVIK and/or the defence exemption add to that risk. Both seem to materialise. Compare federal investment plans in the 2024 budget and medium-term planning (blue line in Exhibit 13) with the 2026 regular budget (grey bars) and SVIK plan and be surprised. The additional investment spending over 2026-28 averages c EUR 18bn or c 0.3-0.4% of GDP per year, including the EUR 8bn transferred to states, where investment spending isn’t assured. That is less than half of what the EUR 500bn SVIK evenly spread over 12y would have promised in total. Put differently, more than half of the additional total spending across categories at the federal level (across the regular budget and Special Purpose Vehicles, SPV) will be in consumption rather than investment components with higher immediate fiscal multipliers, but very low medium-term growth effects. records.text: China Outlook A weaker start Disappointing PMIs point to a weak start to 2026 and suggest that recent front-loaded measures may be insufficient to support sentiment and activity. We expect China to lower its growth target to 4.5-5% this year. The tone from the Trump-Xi call was positive, with Trump confirming his China trip. Disappointing official PMIs point to weaker domestic demand... We think the steep and unexpected contraction in China's January manufacturing PMI points to a weaker start of 2026 following a slowdown in Q4 25, with a significant drop in new orders, a continued decline in the employment index, and a slowing but still-expansionary production index. In contrast to consensus and our forecast for a broadly stable print, the NBS manufacturing PMI fell by 0.8pp, to 49.3 in January. The services PMI also weakened and stayed in contractionary territory for the third consecutive month, indicating subdued services consumption. We think the weaker-than-expected PMIs suggest the recently announced front-loading measures are still insufficient (or may need more time) to stabilize sentiment and growth (see Figure 2 in China: Lower 2026 inflation, 9 January 2026). In particular, on pro-consumption policy, we note the scale of the first batch of the trade-in subsidy program (CNY62.5bn) is ~23% smaller than the level announced in the same period last year (CNY81bn). records.text: US Economics 06 February 2026 Citi Research 2 CPI readings since September have surprised to the downside of consensus expectations, but the takeaway of softening inflationary pressures has been obscured by measurement issues around the government shutdown. Data starting in January should be much less impacted by any measurement issues. Continued softer than expected increases in inflation, especially in January/February when residual seasonality implies more strength, could be more impactful in changing market perceptions around the stickiness to inflation. We expect a 0.30% increase in core CPI in January will be on the softer side of consensus expectations and could be the start of a more convincing slowing in inflation. Goods prices will likely remain stronger than usual, reflecting more pass through of higher tariff costs at a natural time of year to change prices. But we expect details to be more encouraging for underlying inflation having slowed, with services prices this January softer than in previous years. Currently, we are penciling in a 0.30% increase in January core PCE inflation as well, but this will change with CPI details and PPI data. But over January/February data released before the March FOMC meeting, we expect to see less Q1 inflation strength than in previous years that could help convince more hawkish officials that sticky inflation is less of a concern. records.text: M Idea 2 Indonesia Thermal Coal Indonesian government aims to sharply cut production quota on weak thermal coal market dynamics, but uncertainty around enforcement means price reaction has been muted so far. Background Oversupply in the thermal coal market in 2025 led to a sharp downturn in Indonesian coal prices, driven by weak China imports. China consumes ~35% of Indonesian coal exports; however, China's imports from the seaborne market declined at a faster-than-expected rate in 2024-25 (see Exhibit 2 ). Strong domestic coal output growth, particularly in 1H25, and a mild winter 2024-25 led to robust coal stockpiles in China into summer 2025, creating oversupply conditions and weakening import demand. By mid-2025, Indonesian coal prices were down roughly 20% vs the start of the year. The Indonesian government has turned its focus to curbing oversupply, conserving domestic resources and supporting domestic coal prices. A first step on this journey was to shorten the validity of mining production quotas (referred to as RKAB quotas) from three years to one year, which the government announced in early Oct'25. The aim was to give the government more control over output levels and enable them to respond to oversupply conditions more rapidly. This move invalidated quotas for 2026 and 2027, meaning miners had to reapply for quota for this year on a one-year basis. records.text: Post-Election Schedule The schedule following the Lower House general election is as follows. According to the Constitution of Japan, once the Lower House is dissolved and a general election is held, a special session of the Diet must be convened within 30 days of the voting day to appoint the Prime Minister. As the ruling coalition successfully maintained its majority, it is anticipated that Ms. Takaichi would be re-designated as Prime Minister at a relatively early stage, potentially within a few days of the election, and would then proceed to form a new cabinet. To expedite deliberations on the national budget, we think that there would likely be no major reshuffle in cabinet personnel. The special session convened to select the Prime Minister would likely transition directly into deliberations on the budget. It remains uncertain whether the full budget can be passed by the end of the fiscal year (March 31). Should this prove difficult, a provisional or “stopgap” budget would be compiled as necessary, with the goal of passing the main budget for FY2026 sometime after the beginning of April. In early summer, the Basic Policies for Economic and Fiscal Management and Reform are due to be released and set to fully reflect Ms. Takaichi’s expansionary fiscal policy objectives. Meanwhile, the debate around lowering the consumption tax is scheduled to commence within a National Council that will likely be established after the election. Fed-led Warsh to benefit from productivity boom? The main narrative on incoming Chair Warsh has been that he is dovish on rates, but hawkish on the balance sheet. Given that he is also considered a 'credible' central banker, ie, determined to keep inflation anchored, the question is how he would be able to justify the dovishness on rates. His known critique on excessive 'data dependence' already implies that he could try to convince the FOMC to look through the most recent data and be more forward looking. And that forward-looking element could be the anticipation of continuing gains in productivity growth. Recent quarters have already shown some pickup in US productivity growth and the incoming news on ever further progress of new AI applications (eg, Anthropic's new models this week) could suggest much more is to come. An AI-driven productivity revolution in the large services sector would imply a higher potential growth rate, more than offsetting, for example, the immigration-related labour supply reduction. So the narrative goes. But being thoughtfully forward-looking still requires evidence. When Greenspan convinced the Committee to hold off from a rate hike in September 1996 because of productivity, he did so based on a painstakingly detailed analysis of the data. In China, most general AI chatbots, such as DeepSeek and Zhipu, remain free to use to maximize distribution and user acquisition. According to Zhipu's HK IPO filings, Chinese users' willingness to pay for LLMs remains low despite emerging AI assistants and AI tools. As such, it mainly generates revenues from API usage and on-premise LLM deployment from enterprises. For large tech companies, AI monetization comes from Cloud services and API consumption, such as Alibaba and Baidu. These companies earn revenue as enterprise customers scale training, fine-tuning, and inference workloads. Meanwhile, AI is fostering existing business revenues by enhancing ad and search recommendations, powering ad tools for ecommerce, and improving customer services. records.text: TRADE IDEA TRADE IDEA 06/02/2026 1 EM rates: Close paid position in 3y SORA Sources: Bloomberg, Macrobond, BNP Paribas Fig. 1: 3y SORA We close our paid 3y SORA rate trade idea, as it has traded through our stop-loss level. We initiated the idea earlier last month, anticipating a hawkish signal from the Monetary Authority of Singapore. We had expected the MAS to gradually reduce policy accommodativeness through both FX and rates. Our view was based on Singapore experiencing a reflationary phase with robust growth and bottoming-out inflation (see Singapore: Reflation set to change MAS and market views, dated 7 January). Initially, the SORA fixing moved higher, but its inherent volatility makes it challenging to determine whether this represents a sustained trend or a short-term fluctuation (Figure 2). As a result, we suspect that investors may be reducing their paid positions in SORA rates, likely due to the negative carry associated with holding these positions. The MAS did indeed send a hawkish signal at its January meeting, revising up its inflation forecasts and highlighting upside risks to growth and inflation. Although rates initially sold off in the days following the meeting, the recent global selloff in tech stocks, commodities, and cryptocurrencies has led to a broad-based rally across global rates (Figure 1). Although we continue to see a risk that the MAS reduces policy accommodativeness ahead, we respect our stop-loss level and close our H26, 3y SORA idea at 1.562

records.Author: Charlotte Firkins; Amy Gower (Amy Sergeant), CFA; Martijn Rats, CFA; Benjamin Kelson
records.text: l to significantly tighten the seaborne market in 2026. We now model a 9 Mt deficit in 2026, vs our prior 9 Mt surplus. Indonesia commands a leading share of the 4,200–5,000 kcal GAR thermal coal market, leaving lower-energy grades particularly exposed to supply disruptions in the country. Export flows to China, India, and Southeast Asia - regions with a high reliance on Indonesian coal - are expected to bear the brunt of the impact. Importers that rely heavily on spot volumes will also be most exposed, as miners will prioritise exports under long-term contracts. Coastal utilities in India and some Southeast Asian markets that depend on imported Indonesia low cal coal for blending will also face higher prices. This will likely drive a shift towards high-cal coals from South Africa, Australia and Russia. Southeast Asian markets are particularly exposed, as they cannot supplement lost import volumes with higher domestic production as India and China may be able to. Larger, vertically integrated producers in Indonesia with strong domestic market linkages are better equipped to absorb tighter quota regimes, while smaller miners may struggle with higher compliance burdens and rising costs. Overall, the high-cal market will lag any price rises seen in the low-cal market, but substitution effects will likely ensure the entire thermal coal price complex gets uplifted to some degree.

While recently US equity valuations have overshot our macro-implied level, this is in large part because ‘trend inflation’ was still elevated due to COVID-19 shock — using a forward-looking 10-year inflation swap can narrow the gap. At the same time, low nominal growth (in large part due to low inflation), as well as a favourable monetary and fiscal policy regime, resulted in very low bond yields post the GFC — this reversed more recently with better nominal growth and can further explain why equity risk premia have declined so much (Exhibit 16). Combining both models shows that current low equity risk premia have been somewhat linked to those structural macro conditions (Exhibit 17). records.text: M Idea 2 Shining a spotlight on the Fed's footprint The nomination of Kevin Warsh as Chair of the Federal Reserve has renewed focus on the Fed’s presence in financial markets. Warsh has argued that the Fed’s footprint has become excessively large, not only through the absolute size of its asset holdings but also via blurred boundaries between monetary and fiscal policy and an increasingly heavy communications framework that shapes market behavior. While we do not believe his nomination will significantly alter the Fed’s near term interest rate reaction function, it could result in significant shifts in balance sheet strategy, but only in time. We think a rapid shift in the Fed's footprint is unlikely. We outlined the mechanics, constraints, and implications of shrinking the Fed’s footprint in a recent report (see FAQs on a smaller Fed footprint) and summarize those thoughts here. A smaller balance requires reducing bank demand for reserves During the 2022–2025 period, passive QT reduced the balance sheet from roughly $9 trillion to $6.6 trillion, with most of this decline showing up in lower ON RRP balances rather than reserves. Importantly, further balance sheet reduction from here would erode reserves, pushing the system below the boundary from “ample” to “scarce”. Even modest further reduction in the balance sheet from here would begin to put upward pressure on short-term interest rates. records.text: M Update 2 is the missing piece. At the aggregate level, EA productivity growth stands at 0.7%Y in 3Q25. This is modest and not a lot more than the pre-2019 trend (0.6%Y on average in 2015-19). But it is much stronger than one year (0.0%Y in 3Q24) or two years (-1.5%Y in 3Q23) ago. So, what happened? We had flagged in 2024 (see here) that employment did not adjust much to the 2023 activity slowdown. Instead, we were observing significant “labour hoarding”. With that in mind, we expected that increasing activity, at some point, would not mean more (net) job creations, but rather a more intense use of available resources. So are we just seeing a cyclical uptick in productivity? Or is there something more structural here, in the context, for instance, of AI diffusion in the economy? From a macro perspective, one way to check on this is to look into sectoral developments. The data is volatile and prone to revisions. But we think two conclusions stand out. First, stronger aggregate productivity today vs one year ago is due mostly to two sectors: manufacturing and trade, travel & food services. Those are sectors where activity took large hits in the wake of the energy crisis of 2022-23, where we could identify clear signs of “labour hoarding” and which are now recovering (to some extent). records.text: ECB. Swap lines are agreements between two central banks allowing one to obtain another’s currency in exchange for its own, which is provided as collateral. The transaction is reversed at a set date, with the bor- rowed currency repaid plus interest. Many ECB swap lines are reciprocal: the ECB can both provide euro in exchange for foreign currency, and receive foreign currency in exchange for euro, depending on market needs. For instance, euro area banks have used the ECB swap lines with the Fed extensively during past period of crisis such as Lehman, peripheral debt crisis, onset of COVID etc. where banks borrowed USD via these swap lines in exchange for Euros. The ECB/Fed currently offer standing swap lines with maturities of 7D but have extended these to longer horizons during periods of market stress. Repo lines, on the other hand, are arrangements where a central bank borrows foreign cur- rency for a set period, providing high-quality financial assets as collateral. At maturity, the borrowed currency is repaid with interest. Under the ECB’s EUREP (Euro system’s repo facility for central banks) framework, the ECB provides euro to non-euro central banks in exchange for euro-denominated collateral. This facility allows the ECB to provide euro liquidity against adequate collateral when there is heightened demand or risk of euro short- ages. records.text: AI hardware – hyperscalers – operate with high profit margins and ample cash balances, making demand relatively insulated from broader business-cycle fluctuations. Consequently, the current upward semiconductor cycle appears more durable than previous cycles and could extend through 2027, in our view, provided this demand remains intact. Cycle momentum to continue: From a macro perspective, the current electronic cycle is still in an expansionary stage, as AI demand remains robust. Meanwhile, chip manufacturers have taken a more prudent approach on supply management to support their profitability. Yet, we observe a divergence between South Korean and Taiwanese chip inventories: chip makers in the former continue to digest inventory while those in the latter have started to accumulate it. Overall, however, inventories have continued to decline; thus, we see little pressure from inventory accumulation, which should support a continuation of the current expansionary cycle throughout 2026. records.text: We thus instead develop a broader statistical framework to extract the common signal from a range of granular manufacturing datapoints. We do so with a so-called “dynamic-factor model” (or DFM), which assumes that a few unobserved dynamic factors drive the co-movements of a large number of variables. Our model considers monthly growth rates of IP , sales, orders for 24 NACE sectors, the ifo climate indicator at the same level of granularity, as well as truck toll mileage, aggregate sales growth, the headline manufacturing PMI, and core orders at the MIG level, for a total of 82 variables. Each variable is assumed to load on sector-specific factors and on one of two common underlying factors: one is aimed at capturing spot activity momentum and is assumed to drive IP and sales growth, truck toll mileage, ifo climate, and the PMI, while the other loads on orders and is thought to be more forward-looking in nature. Surveys are further assumed to load on a soft-data factor.3 The spot factor mapped into manufacturing IP mom growth evolves much more smoothly than either monthly growth or 3-month average growth rates. It aligns well with phases of strong IP growth such as 2004 to 2008 and 2016/17. Despite its smoothness, it continues to send a timelier signal than year-over-year growth rates (Exhibit 7). 3 The spot and forward factors are assumed to evolve as a joint VAR(2), other factors are assumed to evolve as independent AR(1) processes. Germany—Underlying Manufacturing Dynamics Point to a Recovery Ahead After declining since its peak in 2017/18, the German manufacturing sector showed signs of bottoming out last year. Industrial production and sales have stabilized, and orders have begun to increase. That said, the monthly dataflow remains highly volatile, with the most recent example being the decline in industrial production reported for December, ending three months of firm gains. The rich manufacturing dataflow in Germany—which uniquely comprises orders, sales, and higher-frequency data in addition to industrial production and a range of surveys— further complicates the extraction of a common underlying trend, especially when the signal from different indicators diverge (Exhibit 1). In this week’s Analyst we dig deeper into the German industrial dataflow and propose a framework to separate the signal on the underlying dynamics of German manufacturing from the noise. The Indonesian government has several tiers of regulatory instruments designed to control production, ensure environmental compliance and maintain sufficient coal supply for domestic power consumption. These include: • Company-level mining production quotas (RKAB quotas) approved now on a one- year basis and managed by Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (ESDM). Companies must submit these for government approval via an electronic system. • The Domestic Market Obligation (DMO), which specifies the minimum level of production that must be set aside for the domestic market. It was set at 254 Mt in 2025. These obligations are reliably met each year. The government also sets non-binding production targets each year. The production target sets out the government's overall output aims and indicates its policy direction for the year. However, this is more of a guidance target, with actual production and export levels enforced via the RKAB quotas and DMO. The RKAB quotas are usually higher than the government's production target, as they function as a maximum permitted production level rather than expected production. Leaving headroom with quotas gives miners a degree of flexibility to raise production if market conditions are favourable, without the administrative hurdle of reapplying for new quotas. China's import demand has had a weaker start to the year, which has partially offset any seaborne price rises as Indonesia exports fall. Why LDP won so handily: Most parties campaigned on some form of consumption tax reduction, which blurred their economic-policy differences and turned the election into a personality contest. One reason the LDP added seats is that conservative voters who had drifted to small right-leaning parties, such as the DPP and Sanseito, returned to the LDP after the party installed Sanae Takaichi, the most conservative figure in the LDP, as its leader. In addition, a deteriorating security environment may have heightened the desire for a stable government. Indeed, in the proportional-representation tier, the LDP received enough votes to earn more seats than it had candidates on its party list, so it ceded 14 seats to other parties. In other words, if the party had fielded a larger slate, its total seat count would have been even higher. But even if the LDP had fielded enough candidates, its proportional-representation tally would still be 81 seats— fewer than half of the 176 PR seats in total. KEY MESSAGES Japan’s fiscal policy will become more expansionary after the LDP’s landslide victory in the lower-house election, and a consumption tax cut on food is more likely than not to be implemented, in our view. The victory may amplify Prime Minister Takaichi’s voice and diminish the fiscal-conservative bloc’s influence. There have been three investor strategies to manage US asset dominance: (1) increasing Dollar hedge ratios, (2) diversifying with assets negatively correlated to the Dollar, such as EM assets and Gold, and (3) reducing US asset exposure. After Liberation day, investor focus on FX hedging picked up, especially as the Dollar became more ‘risk on’ and thus exacerbated risk in portfolios — due to the size and liquidity of the US markets, as well as AI optimism, outflows from US assets were very limited. In the second half of 2025 investors were more interested in assets that were negatively correlated with the Dollar —- both EM assets, especially EM/Asia equities, and Gold performed very strongly. However, since the beginning of the year there has been more focus on selectively reducing US asset exposure, both to increased US policy uncertainty and geopolitical concerns, but with less US outperformance — since Q4 the S&P 500 has again underperformed non-US equities materially, more recently due to AI disruption of US mega cap tech stocks. Similar to elevated equity valuations, low carry risk premia alone are not necessarily a warning signal for near-term performance. Carry regimes are closely linked to the business cycle — a high growth score anchors carry risk premia. The growth acceleration in 1H2026 should contain the left tail of carry trades, but the low COI points to more modest carry returns. Exhibit 36 shows the ex ante carry divided by the left-tail risk of carry trades across assets. Adjusted for risk, credit offers little carry pick-up compared with government bonds — tight spreads limit upside but there is material downside in the event of a recession. Carry in EM FX looks attractive, in particular if combined with more cyclical exposures. Our EM strategists expect the more pro-cyclical currencies to outperform given a supportive growth/policy mix in 2026 — they like ZAR and BRL among high yielders (and CPL, KRW among low yielders), paired with funders that can increase carry and resilience, such as EUR, GBP , CAD or SGD (Exhibit 37). That is, January inflation is higher on aver- age, for eight of the eleven remaining months at conventional significance levels. There is strong evidence that December is below January, but December’s average inflation rate is not statistically different from any other month. The results are more mixed for CPI subcomponents: of the remaining months, about one-third for core goods and one- half for core services are statistically below January. Howev- er, once vehicles are excluded from core goods, the differenc- es are starker (Table 1), and the statistical evidence for a January effect is stronger. Excluding rent of shelter from core services also boosts the magnitude of the monthly differences, although the statistical significance across months doesn’t change much. (Rents often adjust annually, but not necessari- ly in January.) records.text: Slowing manufacturing activity at the end of 2025 The euro area manufacturing sector likely ended Q4 on a weak note, with industrial production (excluding construction) contracting by 2.9% m/m in Germany, 0.7% m/m in France and 2.5% m/m in Spain in December. In Germany in particular, output fell sharply in the motor vehicle sector (–6.5% m/m) and in machinery and equipment (–6.8% m/m). While we suspect the December weakness may have been amplified by year-end factory closures not fully accounted for by the seasonal adjustment, the data nonetheless underline how precarious the manufacturing sector’s outlook remains, as manufacturing firms continue to face persistent structural challenges, including a weakening competitive position in both domestic and foreign markets, compounded by a stronger euro and higher US tariffs. Looking ahead, we expect these challenges to persist in the near term, but manufacturing activity should gradually stabilise as the positive impulse from higher infrastructure and defence spending, notably in Germany, begins to filter through the data. Forward-looking indicators support this view: factory orders in Germany posted a fourth consecutive increase in December (+7.8% m/m, after +5.7% m/m in November) to their highest level since February 2022 and closing Q4 with a solid 9.6% q/q rise (2.5% q/q for core orders), with strong gains in defence-related subcategories. The Case for CAD Funding For several months now CAD has been one of our preferred funders, particularly as an option for EM carry expressions. While USD-funded EM carry outperformed last year, we have been arguing that other funders, such as CAD, can neutralize risk exposure and improve the carry-to-vol profile. CAD has one of the highest betas to the broad Dollar. We find that, on a weekly return basis over the past decade, CAD performs in line with safe-haven G10 currencies in broad Dollar moves (Exhibit 1). This illustrates that CAD funding can help lower risk exposure relative to USD, CHF or JPY funding. We’ve also recently shown that CAD funding can increase carry with similar levels of volatility to USD funding. This has been one of the rationales for our standing short CAD/ZAR trade recommendation where we recently raised our total return target to +9%. This could lead to a substantial margin of spare capacity, causing inflation to settle below the 2% target unless monetary policy were loosened further.” Interestingly, once the market settled down, the big move in the distribution of front-end cuts occurred in the near-term MPC meetings (i.e., March and April), with the market now seeing March as the most likely meeting for an additional cut (see Exhibit 6 ). This would be consistent with a gradual (quarterly) pace of easing, although the market still appears uncertain about whether further cuts should be delivered at non-forecast meetings rather than forecast ones. Current valuations still point to a limited probability of sequential (back-to-back) cuts. This could be a tailwind to achieving the top $400bn EBITDA targets, with potential for SpaceX/xAI to be significantly profitable in the latter parts of the 10-year performance period. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 15 Why isn’t JPY strengthening despite BoJ rate hikes and rising yields? To address the initial question, we observe that, in the absence of repatriation flows, a weaker JPY has resulted in higher JGB yields, rather than the opposite. Depreciation of JPY does look to have been driving up expected medium-to-long-term inflation expectations (see Exhibit 23 ), which should not be considered especially surprising with core CPI inflation (all items less fresh food) above +2% for some years now and a further weakening of JPY of course liable to generate additional upward pressure on domestic prices via the import cost channel. Meanwhile, we have yet to see any indication of the BoJ looking to accelerate rate hikes out of concern about inflation overshoot risk. Markets have seemingly responded by pricing a wider term premium into the medium-to-long-term sector on the apparent expectation that the BoJ’s gradual approach to normalization will increase the risk of eventually falling behind the curve (see Exhibit 24 ). The net upshot is that we do indeed appear to be seeing causality running from the exchange rate to interest rates (rather than vice versa) when it comes to JPY. Over just the last year, the enablers are up 25%, the adopters up 15% and those at risk down 35%. AI has clearly become a defining feature of relative stock performance alongside policy drivers like European fiscal stimulus and US tariff policy/currency effects. There aren't many ways to categorise stocks at a macro level with so much of the impact coming down to stock-specifics. Nonetheless, in this report we draw some general conclusions from the stock-specific commentary we are getting through earnings season. What it takes to be an AI 'winner' in Europe Many European companies, especially in capital goods and utilities/renewables, are seeing strong growth from enabling AI expansion. Beyond ASML’s chip-making equipment, firms such as Siemens Energy, Prysmian and Nexans are supplying the turbines and cabling required for data-centres, and all continue to report very strong demand from operators. In practice, we think it would be quite a challenge for the Fed to implement this system given the vast differences in size and business models across banks in the US. We think a more viable alternative to this would be shifting to ‘ceiling’ system for providing reserves, similar to that of the BoE. Under this system, the Fed would reduce reserves up to the point where market participants routinely use ceiling tools such as SRP (formerly SRF) to satisfy their liquidity needs. Adopting this system would result in a reduction of SOMA WAM and effectively convert a portion of the SOMA portfolio into a repo portfolio. However, transitioning to this system also comes with some challenges; for example, the Fed would first need to clear SRP to encourage more usage, as well as combat stigma around its usage. Separately, Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman said last year that she prefers SRP being a backstop instead of a routinely used tool; therefore, reaching FOMC consensus on this topic could be hard. Lastly, while the level of reserves in the system may not decline as much as in the tiering system, we believe Warsh’s main issue with the current size of SOMA is its impact on securities prices and moral hazard. When private credit gets hit, then other institutional investors with exposure to private credit might have an incentive to hedge against a non-linear worsening of the trading momentum, selling other more liquid assets that are correlated with their underlying exposure. This is inevitable to happen and doesn’t necessarily imply a case of overvalued markets. It is the nature of the winner takes all market. Nobody is acting irrationally; it is just the purged effect of the underlying race. The US-China geopolitical race The second more slow moving race is the geopolitical race between the US and China. Both giants competing to become self-sufficient in the production of microchips, the most important input to succeed in the geopolitical race. Whoever becomes self- sufficient first, achieves a strategic advantage from a geopolitical perspective. The outcome of this race or any meaningful accident along the way will also have implications for asset prices, both risky assets and interest rates. records.text: European Airlines: Opportunities in India aviation The exposure of European airlines to the Indian aviation market is modest today. The high market share of the Gulf carriers in the Europe and US market to India market has deterred significant expansion. The Gulf carriers have strong products and low unit costs as they benefit from more favourable labour and taxation environments than European airlines. However, the India government's capacity restraints on Gulf airlines mean that future growth between India and both Europe and North America should fall to the India, European and North American airlines. We think the modest engagement of European airlines since the pandemic reflects the shortage of long haul aircraft and the greater attraction, for airlines, from the strong North American market. European airlines currently maintain relatively limited exposure to India, with service to Indian destinations accounting for a low-single-digit share of their total system-wide capacity. Among the major European flag-carrier groups, in 2025 Lufthansa had the highest proportional exposure (4.1% of ASKs), followed by c3% for IAG and for AF-KLM Group. Notably, some carriers have increased their India presence in the post-pandemic period, reflecting improving demand and strategic repositioning. In addition, the key difference between 1996 and 2026 is that back then, the Fed was facing clear reasons to hike (tight labour market conditions giving rise to higher wage growth). Greenspan argued that productivity estimates at that time were understating underlying growth due to various distortions (eg, due to some price deflators), implying wage growth would not boost unit labour costs as much, in turn dampening the need for a pre-emptive response by the Fed. Today, the question is less about the currently measured productivity growth but more about its outlook: how much productivity will rise and how persistent the increase will be. These questions are harder to answer with conviction than those faced by Greenspan. The evidence today certainly offers some signs of a sustained pickup in productivity growth. After sharp pandemic-related swings, the last two years show productivity rates in the corporate sector fluctuating at higher levels than pre-COVID, and possibly accelerating. As benchmark revisions to payrolls next week are likely to revise down total hours worked, this should mechanically further boost current estimates of productivity. records.text: (5) How would you protect portfolios from more frequent geopolitical shocks? The first line of defense for more geopolitical shocks should be robust portfolio construction, as timing around those is very difficult, but we also like selective hedges. Geopolitical and political shocks pose significant risks to investment portfolios, yet their unpredictable nature makes them challenging to anticipate or position for. These events often begin locally but can escalate to have global and long-lasting effects. The broader macro backdrop also matters — geopolitical shocks can result in higher equity volatility with weak macro conditions but matter less otherwise (Exhibit 21). Currently, a robust US economy and Fed put may help absorb such shocks. The impact of geopolitical crises also varies across asset classes; for example, past Middle East conflicts led to surging oil prices and weaker global growth, but recent tensions have not driven oil higher given excess supply. Instead, recent shocks have seen investor unease reflected more in a weaker US Dollar and stronger Gold prices. records.text: At the April meeting, the BoJ will have access to the initial results of annual spring wage negotiations (aka “shunto”), as well as the April Tankan and information from the branch managers’ meeting. The latter will allow it to assess, to some extent, how December’s rate hike has affected funding conditions among SMEs. Therefore, any perception that an April hike is purely a response to JPY weakness could be somewhat mitigated. We see two-way risk to the prospect of an April rate hike. If JPY depreciation accelerates further and intervention becomes difficult, a rate hike at the March meeting cannot be ruled out. On the other hand, if the China-related risks triggered by Takaichi’s comments on a possible Taiwan contingency visibly materialize, the BoJ may need to lower its growth and inflation projections or cite a downward skew to its risk balance in the April Outlook Report. This could push it toward a wait-and-see stance. These risks consist of weaker inbound consumption and export restrictions on dual-use products including rare earths; if prolonged or worsened, the former would likely affect the inflation outlook in particular, while the latter would have a non- negligible impact primarily on the economic outlook. The upward revision of our terminal rate forecast (from 1.25% to 1.5%) reflects the growing likelihood of a prolonged Takaichi administration, which would increase the possibility of a more persistent JPY depreciation bias, in our view. records.text: 3 Insights Information Classification: General About PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. In our view, the likelihood of a consumption tax cut, a pledge made by nearly all n parties including the ruling coalition, has significantly increased based on the election result. While details will be discussed in a cross-party “National Council,” we expect the ruling coalition’s proposal for a temporary two-year tax cut on food items only to form the basis of the discussion following its landslide victory. Although uncertainty remains regarding funding and timing, we believe that as long as the tax cut is a temporary measure, it would not cause a significant deterioration in Japan’s fiscal position. However, as restoring the tax rate once it has been lowered could be politically difficult, there is a high possibility that the tax cut will eventually become permanent. We believe that if a permanent consumption tax cut was combined with increased defense spending and rising interest payments, the risk of the government debt-to-GDP ratio shifting to a long-term upward trend would increase. We believe the Bank of Japan’s (BOJ) stance is shifting from its previous cautious n approach to one oriented toward steady policy rate hikes. records.text: ey downside tail for rent inflation is that vacancy continues to drift higher – not necessarily because construction reaccelerates, but rather because the supply impulse lasts longer than implied by starts and completions, which are flows. While starts and completions are observable flows, it is the balance of the rental stock versus renters that matters. The rental stock is harder to measure in real time. If completions stay firm for longer, absorption slows or renter growth softens, the vacancy rate could edge up further. In that scenario, the supply impulse would prove more persistent than we assume and could pull rent inflation lower than our base case, extending the disinflation phase. records.text: Basic Policies for Economic and Fiscal Management and Reform will be announced, and we think the government is likely to push for a major fiscal package. There is likely to be a return to talk of calculating the primary balance over a number of fiscal years. Based on MoF estimates as of January 2025, there will be a decline in issuance of refinancing bonds between FY3/28 and FY3/31. The current profile has changed somewhat with increases in issuance of 2y and 5y bonds, but maintaining the scale of current issuance would provide sufficient funding. Naturally, debt servicing costs are a consideration given that interest rates are rising. The Cabinet Office’s Economic and Fiscal Projections for Medium to Long Term Analysis also point to a steady transition to r>g, so the rise in interest rates as debt is refinanced will quickly erode the fiscal buffer. As a result, we expect it to be April-June when volatility rises. Even if there is no problem with fiscal year-end funding, the market could have a negative reaction to growth in the budget deficit over the longer term. LLC Global Markets Daily: The Case for CAD Funding 6 February 2026 | 7:25AM EST CAD has been one of our preferred funders given its high beta to the broad n Dollar and its added ability to lower risk exposure and increase carry with similar levels of volatility to USD funding. Recently, commodity price volatility has been an increasingly important driver of FX. In this Global Markets Daily we assess the potential risks to CAD through the lens of oil market dynamics. While CAD has been broadly supported by the rally in oil prices in recent weeks—n and a key risk to CAD funding remains a continued trend higher—our commodity strategists expect oil prices to decline, assuming no supply disruptions. This should weigh on CAD because it is one of the currencies most sensitive to an oil price shock on our GSTOT framework. Beyond the tactical terms of trade impulse, we find that major shifts in oil prices n tend to correspond to periods where the correlation between CAD and the broad Dollar break down. The potential for a resumption of oil exports to the US from Venezuela could be another catalyst, though stylized estimates of the ultimate FX impact are modest, implying a ~1% increase in USD/CAD using an external balance approach or CAD’s typical sensitivities to oil prices. As in other aging economies, the current surplus has been well-recycled into overseas investment (Figure 22) – led by institutional and retail investors – sparking persistent KRW weakness in the last few years. We expect that trend to reverse this year on the following factors: ▪ Resistance to further KRW depreciation: KRW weakness has caught the authorities' attention, given financial stability concerns, and we have seen rounds of smoothing efforts that managed to cap USDKRW topside. With authorities showing determination to stabilize FX, we think residents’ depreciation expectations have likely faded meaningfully. ▪ Solid base: The memory super-cycle should offer a strong support for the current account surplus, a key KRW fundamental. Meanwhile, the currency has tended to appreciate in an upward electronics cycle, suggesting the current environment may be supportive for lower USDKRW, alongside a gradually lower USDRMB. ▪ Government efforts to boost KOSPI: We think current policies are seeking to guide long-term capital into local equities, from both domestic and foreign investors. records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 06 February 2026 5 Main contents and schedule for the 2025‑base year revision According to the “2025 base-year revision plan” released by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC) released last November, the main elements of the CPI rebasing are as follows. 1. Revisions to CPI reference period and weights: The index reference period (annual period for which the index is set to 100) is to change from 2020 to 2025. The basis of weightings for each item in the CPI are to also change from average household expenditure amounts for 2019-20 to average amounts for 2025. 2. Revision to CPI Items: Nineteen items are to be newly added, eleven items will be removed, and two items will be consolidated into one (see Exhibit 13). Certain item names are to be updated to reflect current usage. 3. Wider use of POS data: Amid growth in online shopping in recent years, the CPI is to expand its use of point-of sales (POS) data. 4. Model revisions: For items with complex pricing structures such as airfares, electricity bills and mobile phone service fees, the model formulas used to compute prices are to be revised. The target items and the CPI impact are yet unknown. The 2025-base methods are to take effect from the July nationwide CPI (released on 21 August). records.text: 4 Japan Macro Watch | 09 February 2026 Looking ahead, focus is expected to turn to the appointment of a successor to BOJ Policy Board member Noguchi, whose term expires on March 31. According to a Reuters report on January 13, the Japanese government is expected to present its nominee for Noguchi’s successor after the special parliamentary session convenes. Prime Minister Takaichi has previously signaled openness to BOJ policy rate hikes, but given the LDP’s landslide victory in the lower house election, the possibility remains that she could again lean toward reflationary policies. Indeed, on January 31, Prime Minister Takaichi praised the yen’s recent depreciation for boosting exporters and increasing returns on the government’s foreign‑exchange reserves. If an individual known to be a reflationist is nominated as Noguchi’s successor, the market’s terminal‑rate assumption - currently around 1.75% - is likely to be pushed lower. As a hedge against this scenario, we see a costless 6m5y receiver ladder as an appropriate strategy. Post-election price action a little difficult to predict due to the market uncertainty A consumption tax cut might appear to be inevitable given that it is supported by both sides of the Diet. But market expectations are more complex. For starters, some market participants believe that fiscal discipline will be the key policy theme in the event of an LDP victory, with super-long JGBs accordingly having seen a certain amount of support of late. Such views appear to reflect an assessment that Japan will find it difficult to justify fiscal expansion to the international community in the wake of the New York Fed having reportedly conducted a so-called 'rate check' in the USD/JPY market, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent having expressed concerns about possible spillovers from higher JGB yields, and the Treasury Department’s latest semiannual “Report on Macroeconomic and Foreign Exchange Policies of Major Trading Partners of the United States” having also made mention of “expansionary fiscal policies”. Prime Minister Takaichi has not commented on a consumption tax cut, which has also supported the view that there could be a withdrawal of the proposal of a consumption tax cut after the election. We continue to assume the auto sector absorbs a larger share of tariff costs, reflecting a combination of (i) stronger affordability constraints, (ii) less tariff-exposed manufacturers pursuing market share, and (iii) more tariff-exposed manufacturers holding out for tariff relief. Exempting autos from tariff pass-through reduces the total potential addition to consumer prices to about 0.7pp on our current tariff estimates. Putting these pieces together, our baseline is that the remaining tariff impulse should show up primarily through core goods ex. autos and continue to do so gradually. Extrapolating last year’s realized pace implies that firms recoup most of the remaining tariff burden over the course of 2026 – equivalent to roughly 0.4pp of additional upward pressure on consumer prices, of which about 0.3pp should come through the goods sector. records.text: 6 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 56 Deutsche Bank AG Bund yield = neutral rate + term premia Today we revisit a previous FICOTD published last September where we approximated the 10y Bund yield’s variation via 2y1y ESTR (proxy for nominal neutral rate) and 5s10s DBRs term premia (i.e. 5s10s + 0.2 x 2s, using German yields). The point we made back then is that the front-end has been the main driver of Bund yields lately, and this continues to be the case in 2026. When it comes to the 5s10s TP, as is clearly shown in the chart, there was a one-off adjustment higher in March 2025 following the announcement of the German fiscal regime change and since then it has moved within a very tight range, not contributing to the Bund yield’s variation much. Our year-end target for DBRs 5s10s TP is around 10bp higher than current levels, hence we anticipate a slow and gradual drift higher, in line with the move we’ve seen since November last year. For the record, our TP target is a bit conservative since it’s roughly around the minimum value seen in the pre-ECB QE era. Instead, if we replace the minimum with the average TP value in the same period, this can lead to an even higher 5s10s TP level by roughly an additional 10bp. On the contrary, the 2y1y ESTR has been much more volatile throughout the past year, mainly driven by the German fiscal news in March, Liberation day tariffs in April, drop in oil prices in October and hawkish ECB meeting in December. Reading the tea leaves of real GDP growth at the start of the year The signal from high frequency indicators, both soft and hard data, is of positive growth but less strong than in Q4 25, when momentum had already soften from the beginning to the end of the quarter. Growth remains uneven across sectors and countries. In Germany, new orders data and PMIs sub-categories provide evidence that defence and infrastructure spending is increasing, but activity continued to contract in other sectors, in particular motor vehicles and construction. Euro area retail sales also dropped in December (-0.5% m/m), and the November print was revised to the downside (0.1% m/m, 0.2% m/m previously). Moreover, real-time job ads of STOXX 600 companies indicate that overall hiring momentum has flattened (for more, see Data Science: European labour demand from job ads). The spread signal is calculated as the ratio of the current spread relative to the prior one-year median spread. The values are then smoothed using a 20-day moving average. For example, a multiple of 1 indicates that the current average spread is equal to the historical median spread for that currency pair, whereas a multiple reading of 2 indicates that the current average spread for that given currency pair is twice as wide as its historical median. Turbulence is a price-based measure of the joint unusualness of G10 currency returns. It captures spikes in volatility in individual market components as well as correlation breakdowns – atypical co-movements – between these components. records.text: Carlin Doyle 6 February 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General EM Inf lation in Focu s : Push and Pull Fuel vs Food. Most EM central banks have either finished cutting interest rates or are in the late stages of the easing cycle. In part this reflects soft domestic demand, but mostly as a result of lower fuel prices. In spite of geopolitical risk, EM fuel prices reflect a low volatility in oil prices that has characterized most of the past year. As a result, the PriceStats EM Fu el price aggregate has been negative yoy since April 2025 (Figure 1). That said, EM is not entirely clear of all infl ation risks. In some economies, including Turkey, economic growth is running hot. Elsewhere, higher food price s have countered the benefits of lower oil prices with aggregate food inflation still hovering at 7%yoy. Many market commentators have pointed to Friday’s selloff in silver as a combination of strong retail engagement on the way up, combined with dealer gamma on the way down. We think the two could be intertwined. Early 2026 saw massive leveraged (both positively and inversely) silver ETF volumes, most likely from retail investors. These daily volumes dwarfed volumes relative to 2025, where retail participation was strong (Figure 29). This is an interesting dynamic because leveraged ETFs drive rebalancing flows, and this rebalancing is inherently short gamma. ETF rebalance requirements scale positively with the square of the ETF’s leverage factor, the size of the move in the underlying, and the AUM of the fund. As such, we can construct rough estimates of daily rebalancing requirements attributable to leveraged ETFs (Figure 30). We estimate that, last Friday, leveraged ETF rebalancing was responsible for selling ~$5bn worth of silver, a dramatic increase from historical flows which, pre-2026, were negligible. records.text: Compute Layer/Capex In this section we attempt to map out the total annual token usage and the size of GPU clusters needed for China’s leading AI players to service its inference and training needs. We adopt a bottom-up approach which categorizes each company's token usages into three buckets. 1) 1P application inference, 2) Public cloud MaaS (Mode as a Service) usage, and 3) Internal model training. • 1P application inference captures token usage within each company’s standalone AI assistants (e.g., Bytedance’s Doubao, Tencent’s Yuanbao) and AI features embedded within their high-traffic apps (e.g., AI search in Tencent’s Wechat and Bytedance’s Douyin). We estimate 1P application currently drives the majority of inference volume for Chinese AI players. • Public cloud MaaS reflects the commercialization of models to third-party enterprise clients. It aggregates token usage generated by external API calls (e.g., BABA’s Bailian, Bytedance’s Volcengine). Although growing at a rapid speed, this remains a small % of overall token usage. • Internal training represents the “fixed” computational cost for these companies. It encompasses the token consumption required for pre-training foundation models, as well as continuous post-training and fine-tuning. Beyond the tactical terms of trade impulse, CAD’s sensitivity to oil prices could point to a more sustained headwind for the currency. As mentioned above, CAD has one of the highest betas to the Dollar, but there are certain circumstances when CAD can move against the general Dollar trend. We find that major shifts in oil prices tend to correspond to periods where the close relationship between CAD and the broad Dollar breaks down (Exhibit 4). While this is largely a function of shifting global growth expectations, significant oil price shocks can serve as a differentiating driver of CAD and oil prices trending lower in line with our commodity strategists’ forecasts could drive CAD underperformance vs the broad Dollar. The potential for a resumption of oil exports to the US from Venezuela as suggested by the recent energy deal could be another catalyst for CAD underperformance. Key Takeaways JPY is not behaving as 'higher JGB yields = a stronger JPY'. Instead, the dominant pattern is 'a weaker JPY = rising JGB yields', reflecting higher inflation expectations. The risk of repatriation by domestic investors tends to be overstated. Constraints vary by investor type, and those constraints drive actual flows. Recent JPY weakness is explained less by securities flows and more by speculation/carry trades. For JPY to appreciate, we think either global risk sentiment must deteriorate (risk- off) or concerns about Japan’s fiscal expansion must ease. FX intervention – especially speculation about coordinated intervention – is a non-linear risk, easily triggering higher volatility and position unwinds. We see a non-negligible possibility of USD/JPY falling to around 145 – roughly 'fair value' – at least temporarily in such a scenario. A key ingredient of the EA macro outlook is the labour market, and sure enough, a question on that topic was raised at the ECB press conference yesterday (here). Let’s use this weekly to refresh our views. Seen from afar, the EA labour market looks solid. At 6.2% in Dec-25, the unemployment rate stands at an historical low. And it has been very stable since mid-2024, hovering between 6.2 and 6.4%. However, a closer look reveals some recent, less positive developments. In 3Q25 (as President Lagarde stressed yesterday, EA labour market data are quite lagged), total employment was running at a growth rate of 0.6%Y. This is significantly less than just one (1.0%Y in 3Q24) or two years (1.5%Y in 3Q23) ago. We had flagged already in our 2026 outlook in November (here) that this slowdown is matched by lower growth of the labour force. So, the stable EA unemployment rate masks less tepid demand and weak supply of labour. (Our focus here is on the euro area. German construction PMIs declined in January to 44.7 from 50.3 in December, pointing to a sharp contraction in housing (Jan: 36.9, Dec: 48.1) and commercial activity (Jan: 40.3, Dec: 43.9), while activity in civil engineering fell by less and remained above the 50 mark indicating expansion (Jan: 56.4, Dec: 57.5). Inflation fell below target in January on energy base effects and softer services Euro area HICP inflation fell by 0.3pp in the January flash estimate, easing to 1.7% y/y, while core inflation edged down by 0.1pp to 2.2% y/y. The decline in headline inflation was driven mainly by a deeper drag from energy prices (–4.1% y/y, compared with –1.9% y/y in December), alongside softer services inflation (3.2% y/y, down from 3.4% y/y in December), potentially reflecting weaker January price resets. Meanwhile, core goods inflation was broadly stable (+0.1pp to 0.4% y/y), and food, alcohol and tobacco inflation rose to 2.7% y/y (from 2.5% in December). Across countries, headline inflation decelerated year-on-year in most major euro area economies, and dispersion among member states appears to be gradually diminishing (Figure 1 and Figure 2): HICP inflation stood at 2.5% y/y in Spain, 2.1% y/y in Germany, 1.0% y/y in Italy and just 0.4% y/y in France. records.text: Timing the market impact of geopolitical events is particularly difficult given usually high uncertainty and multiple potential outcomes, including a reversal of the shock. Historical data shows that equities often recover and sometimes rally strongly once uncertainty eases or policies change, as witnessed after Liberation day in April last year (Exhibit 22). Therefore, robust portfolio construction and diversification remains the primary defense, with balanced multi-asset portfolios and selective allocations to safe haven assets such as bonds or the Swiss Franc providing some protection, though these come with their own trade-offs and limitations. To further buffer against geopolitical risks, investors may consider increasing allocations to assets that benefit from heightened uncertainty, such as Gold, precious metals, or defense stocks, while remaining aware that their long-term returns can be modest. Reducing exposure to regions or sectors vulnerable to specific shocks, and managing FX risk through a greater home bias, can also be prudent strategies. Given the rapid and sometimes short-lived nature of geopolitical shocks, option volatility is valuable, especially when market volatility is low, though the cost of such protection may limit its use. records.text: Factor 3: Storage, Futures, and Physically Backed Instruments When financial flows push prices above fundamentals, higher supply and lower demand can result in inventory accumulation until hitting storage capacity limits. Storage Limits and Futures Roll Costs. Storage capacity limits are typically lower for energy (and agriculture) than for easy-to-store metals.6 Hitting storage constraints (“tank tops”) can substantially reduce roll returns7 on energy futures and trigger price corrections, as happened in oil markets in 2020. In contrast, roll costs tend to remain limited on futures for easy-to-store metals such as copper (Exhibit 5), and don’t exist when owning physically backed assets such as precious ETFs. 6 Commodities that are harder to store (e.g. power, natural gas) also have more volatile prices. 7 The roll return on commodities futures—the difference between the spot price and the futures price—is the return that comes from rolling from a futures contract that is about to expire to one with a later expiration. While the initial reaction would likely be bull flattening, we expect the stance towards consumption tax hikes to act as a headwind, gradually unwinding part of the yield decline over time. Scenario analysis: Where’s 'fair' for long-term interest rates? Amid such uncertainty we offer a guide to 30y ASW, 30y OIS and 30y JGB 'fair value' in two possible scenarios for the election. In this analysis, we consider two polar scenarios: one in which the LDP wins by a large margin and another in which it suffers a major defeat. Of course, several intermediate scenarios are also conceivable, such as the ruling coalition securing a majority together with Ishin, or expanding the coalition further to maintain a majority. The purpose of this analysis is to illustrate where the fair value range would lie in these two extreme outcomes. If the lower bound of the fair value range suggests only limited room for yields to decline relative to current levels, while the upper bound indicates substantial upside risk to yields, then from a risk/reward perspective we believe that investors should adopt a bearish stance on rates. In addition, intermediate scenarios present technical challenges, as it becomes difficult to specify the necessary assumptions for the explanatory variables used in the estimation. Let’s go back to the state of the labour market. We have a stable unemployment rate but slowing labour demand. How should we think about this in terms of labour market tightness? records.text: The notable divergence across Chinese macro indicators reflects the structural transformation the government has pursued: reducing reliance on the property market and promoting technology, innovation, and high-tech manufacturing for improved productivity and growth. We believe this cross-industry divergence is here to stay. Strong performance in exports and IT does not mean government support in these areas will end. Lesson #3: High-tech advancement broadening, property market drag peaking China’s aggressive push in high-tech manufacturing is showing results. Between 2023 and 2025, not only did the “new three” sectors (electric vehicles, lithium-ion batteries, and solar panels) see sharp production increases, but output of power generating equipment, packaging machinery, industrial robots, ships, and semiconductors also rose significantly (Exhibit 5). Exhibit 6 is a stylized diagram that illustrates the ongoing economic restructuring. It highlights two transformation stages. In the first stage, when innovation and rapid growth were limited to a few sectors like the “new three”, the drag from the severe property downturn outweighed the boost from high-tech manufacturing, requiring additional government policies to stabilize overall growth. Over time, the economy should enter the second stage, where the property drag fades and technological innovation spreads across many manufacturing and business services sectors, resulting in a more positive total impact on GDP growth. AI can automate coding, support, and matching tasks, which can push prices down and reduce the amount of human work clients are willing to pay for unless these firms create more AI-powered products or outcome-based services. Gatekeepers AI can route around  Rightmove, Auto Trader: AI tools can gather information from many websites at once, which reduces the need for companies to pay these platforms for listings or visibility unless the platforms prove they deliver better quality leads or unique verified data that AI tools can’t replace. Advertising & content deflation  WPP , ITV: AI drastically lowers the cost of making ads and creative content. This means clients may spend less, shift work in-house, or use automated tools, reducing revenues for companies dependent on traditional ad production or legacy TV formats unless they grow newer AI-driven offerings. IP/rights exposure  Ubisoft, Pearson: AI can generate game art, characters, lessons, and educational content that competes with these companies’ proprietary material. If they don’t control how their content is used in AI training or don’t develop authenticated, premium AI products, their existing IP loses value. A key point to watch is a potential shift in the Prime Minister's policy management style. After calling the election, Takaichi had hinted at a willingness to listen to signals from financial markets—particularly the yen's depreciation and rising long- term interest rates—and fine-tune her fiscal policy stance accordingly. However, with the strong public mandate from this landslide victory, it remains to be seen whether she will prioritize her own policies more boldly over short-term market reactions or continue to emphasize dialogue with the market. This change will be a crucial indicator of her administration's approach to economic management. Furthermore, the fact that the CRA, the only major party to clearly call for a correction of the weak yen, failed to gain support suggests that public backlash against the yen's depreciation may not be as strong as some have feared.
