records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 06 February 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS A tale of 3 races It is no longer a secret that the K-shaped dynamics of consumption, more markedly evidenced in the US but taking place more broadly at a global level, are becoming increasingly dependent on the strong performance of financial and real assets. In the meantime, the world is witnessing 3 races with important implications for risky assets and interest rates: 1) the AI race; 2) the US-China geopolitical race and 3) the private vs public race for funding. They are all interconnected and are all critical to understand the potential multiple equilibria the global economy might end up landing. We analyze them in turn. The AI race We start here because that is where the market focussed this week. The AI revolution, like many other tech developments in the past, is a winner takes all kind of market. It needs network externalities to work. We are all better off if we use the same technology. It creates a race to take over the global market. In that race, there will be, inevitably, winners and losers. What we are starting to see in the market is that investors are starting to punish those software companies that are perceived as the weakest link in this race. The problem gets exacerbated because many of these projects are being financed by private credit, illiquid by nature. (7) Is US asset dominance in portfolios still a concern and how are investors managing it? Yes, US assets remain dominant in global benchmarks, and investors continue to focus on more FX hedging, diversification to assets negatively correlated with the Dollar and reducing US exposure selectively. US assets remain dominant in global multi-asset portfolios after gaining more weight since the GFC, in large part due to US asset outperformance – the US has more than a 60% weight in global equity and near 50% in bond benchmarks, which gives it more than 50% in the World Portfolio benchmark (Exhibit 26). In line with the World Portfolio, we find investors currently have higher allocations to US assets, with the weight having picked up materially since the GFC. Based on recent data, US asset allocations have not declined much (Exhibit 27) — they dipped last year in large part due to the weaker Dollar and less US equity outperformance. records.text: f volatility in the super-long JGB market has seemingly been supported in part by Prime Minister Takaichi’s approach to the consumption tax. In other words, the fact that she has not made any statements on the consumption tax is being interpreted by the market as a sign that the likelihood of a tax cut has diminished. Furthermore, we believe that market expectations for potential policy action by the MoF have also contributed to stabilizing the super-long sector. Following the sharp rise in super-long JGB yields, Finance Minister Katayama spoke in a Bloomberg interview to the effect that “we have taken steps to stabilize the market, and I can assure you that we will continue to do so”. This led to the market questioning whether the MoF could take policy measures such as cutting issuance, contributing to the calming of volatility in the super-long sector. In practice, there are no signs the MoF is moving towards policy action, but expectations for such a response remain deep-rooted and appear to act as a buffer against upward pressure on yields. That said, against the backdrop of strong demand from overseas investors, the perceived need to take additional immediate policy action has diminished.

records.text: 5 Figs. 9 and 10: GDP growth relative to previous averages Source: BNP Paribas South Korea: We raise our 2026 GDP growth forecast to 2.3% from 2.0%, and lift our 2027 forecast to 1.9% from 1.8%. We expect the output gap to stay in negative territory, albeit to a lesser degree as growth rises faster than recent trends (Figure 9). Domestic demand will be critical in the coming years. We expect an increase in its contribution to growth compared to 2025, with consumption likely supported by wealth effects and base effects, as well as by expansionary fiscal budgets – although we note downside risks from an increased loan-repayment burden. On investments, we expect modest momentum. Construction investment could be supported by an increase in orders, SOC spending by the government and AI-related infrastructure investment, but we remain cautious on the speed of the rebound due to structural factors. As we discussed previously, labor market turnover has decreased sharply over the past few years, and the consequences fall disproportionately on young workers who are entering the labor force for the first time. As shown in the left panel of Exhibit 3, both the layoff rate and in particular the hiring rate stand below their 2019 averages. This low-hire, low-fire trend has likely contributed to the rise in the unemployment rates of young workers shown in Exhibit 2 and raises the risk that these workers might be increasingly locked out of the labor market. Indeed, the right panel of Exhibit 3 shows that unemployed workers aged 16-35 in states with the largest declines in labor market turnover have experienced larger increases in the length of their unemployment spells than young workers in states with smaller declines in turnover. The share of respondents that are optimistic or very optimistic about the prospects for the country printed at 65% in Cadem's latest survey, the highest since the beginning of the Piñera administration in early 2018 and up 35 points compared to late 2024. The implications of this optimism are twofold. On the positive side, we expect the accompanying boost in business and consumer sentiment to support investment and consumption. We expect 3.0% nonmining growth this year, also helped by record-high copper prices and strengthening real wages. This would be above the prepandemic (2014-19) average of 2.2%. On the other hand, these expectations set a high bar for Kast. The day-to-day efficacy of his administration will be under scrutiny, and competent management and political maneuvering will be key to sustain this momentum in sentiment and to pass laws (such as the reduction in the corporate tax). The first test has been the construction of his cabinet. Kast devoted one- third of the cabinet to cement the relationship with the political wing of his coalition and two- thirds to trusted, more-technical profiles. This balance seems reasonable to attend both politics and policy management. Another crucial determinant of Kast's political success would be his ability to build coalitions in Congress. We added a long carry BRLJPY dual digi in 12 Themes of Christmas (15-Dec- 25), USDJPY > 160, USDBRL < 5.30, expiring mid-March. Rates: most roads lead to higher terminal BoJ rate, so belly should underperform. As we mentioned last week, we expect the BoJ to continue its normalization cycle, even as the pace is uncertain. The 25bp hike dissent in the last BoJ meeting is reminiscent of the September BoJ meeting, when board members Takata and Tamura voted for a 25bp hike, then executed after the LDP election in December. Currently, market expects the next hike after the elections in April. With respect to JPY depreciation, while it impacts imported inflation, we note that the JPY FX impact on inflation has fallen in recent years as USDJPY has remained rangebound, as shown in Figure 23 via the BoJ’s import price series disaggregated by FX impact. records.text: 6 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 35 UK Gilt Issuance We provide the upcoming gilt auction calendar together with cash flow dynamics for the next quarter. In the UK, there will be an auction of conventional 4.125% Mar 2031 and tender sale of 4.25% Dec 2049 next week. In the following week, there will be a tender sale of conventional gilt at the short or medium end. Gross gilt supply in the next two weeks should be ~ £4.7bn in cash terms and ~£2.4mn/bp in DV01 terms. In terms of cash flow, with gilt sales from the APF portfolio by the BoE and coupon payment to market in the next week , gilt net supply (supply - coupon to market + active QT) should be ~£3.1mn/bp in DV01 terms for the next two weeks. Ahead of that, shortly after the end of the reference month, Destatis releases its monthly truck toll mileage index, which measures the mileage covered by large toll-paying trucks on German motorways and correlates well with IP growth (Exhibit 2). The two main surveys on manufacturing activity are the PMI and the ifo survey, which feeds into the European Commission’s business survey. Given the larger sample size, the ifo manufacturing survey is released at a more granular level, allowing analysis at the two-digit industry level, while the PMI can only be disaggregated into three major industrial groupings. Both surveys are released between 10 and 5 days before the end of the reference month and are thus timelier than hard-data indicators. Simple correlations suggest that changes in the ifo Business Climate index display the highest contemporaneous correlation with monthly IP growth.1 But the PMI indicators are more suitable as leading indicators for future IP growth (Exhibit 3). 1 While PMI questions ask about changes in activity or orders, the ifo question on business conditions asks companies whether the situation is good, satisfactory, or poor. This suggests that changes in the ifo business conditions index—as opposed to its level—might be more informative for IP growth. The answer to the second question was in Deputy Governor Breeden's voting paragraph. The change in tone around the risks to the inflation outlook stemmed from the Bank Staff's new analysis, not any new data. This new analysis, we think, is the key takeaway of today's meeting, as it points to a change in the Bank's framework. Put it differently, on the surface, the meeting was broadly in line with our expectations. Under the hood, the apparent sea change in the structural assessments came as a surprise to us. The new analyses: Where last year saw the MPRs overflowing with references to "structural shifts in pay and price setting processes", with the Feb-25 supply-side stock-take embedding structurally negative productivity growth, today's analyses looks similar to our long-standing views. Inflationary process in the UK looks largely unscathed by a string of post-2020 supply-side shocks. Productivity growth looks to be on a cyclical upswing. Target-consistent pay growth is a smidge above 3%, and pay settlement surveys are broadly consistent with attaining and maintaining the 2% inflation target. The Bank can focus on the real economy, as long as the disinflationary progress continues. The VARX, in which we input our baseline forecasts, differs little from the endogenous VAR. Why we shade modestly lower than the VAR in 2026: While the VAR’s qualitative message (no crater; trough, then stabilization) matches our view, we shade our 2026 path modestly lower for three reasons. First, the post-pandemic supply impulse was unusually large by historical standards and may be underweighted. The completion pipeline and local supply overhangs could maintain incremental pressure on rents longer than implied by the VAR. Second, we put somewhat more weight on the recent downtick in market rents, which continues to point to additional CPI rent disinflation through the lag window. Third, we see downside asymmetry in demand formation (notably via immigration) that is difficult to parameterize cleanly inside the VAR, but is directionally relevant for 2026. Nonetheless, applying this modestly cooler forecast only knocks off about 0.3pp from core CPI inflation this year – just enough to offset the incremental heat from higher goods inflation while non-shelter services remains steady. Federal states in the headlines - significant changes unlikely Financial equalization between German federal states amounted to EUR 20bn in 2025, with Bavaria - by far the largest payer state - paying a record EUR 11.7bn. In total, twelve of the sixteen federal states are receiver states, leading to significant criticism from the payer states. Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg, and Hesse have publicly complained about the system and now ask for an absolute limit regarding the re-distribution and have threatened to resign from the current system in 2030. However, the federal state of Hamburg - which is a small payer state - publicly committed to the current system. In our view, most of this is likely just political noise, for example, driven by upcoming federal state elections in Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg. The German Basic Law (Grundgesetz, GG) requires broadly equal ("gleichwertige") living conditions in all the 16 German federal stages. For this, the financial equalization system will remain necessary. Significant changes seem unlikely and even impossible in the short term. Hence, we view these headlines as nothing to worry about for investors in bonds of supposedly weaker federal states regarding stand-alone credit quality. Hence, the cumulative residual of each country's spread is zero over that 1-year sample. We also show the change in these residuals over the past 5/10/20 days to identify which spreads have been richening/cheapening lately. By construction, if there is a structural repricing of a country's spread (for example due to political uncertainty), this country's spread would appear cheap while other countries' spreads would richen. Its level now lies well below those consistent with the less volatile estimate from Indeed.com, which has moved sideways since September (Figure 2). Given indicators on hand, our Alternative Data Signal models point to some of the JOL TS openings estimate in January, especially using signals from Indeed.com (Figure 5). We are similarly skeptical about the signal from the latest initial jobless claims estimates for the week ended January 31, which showed a 22k jump from the prior week, to 231k, in seasonally adjusted terms. Although we will be keeping an eye on upcoming readings, we tend to discount the latest reading given that the largest increases were focused in Rust Belt states that were experiencing unusually cold weather. Even if we take this at face value, it remains well within the range of seasonally adjusted readings during Q4 2025 and is only somewhat above the range typically seen in late January, prior to adjustments (Figure 3). records.text: Of course, this framework does not capture everything that can trigger an equity bear market — it combines valuations and the business cycle set-up with macro momentum such as leading economic indicators and risk clustering. Current elevated valuations point to continued bear market risk but the favourable business cycle setup of above-trend growth, falling inflation and policy easing, coupled with a pick-up in leading indicators and anchored volatility, currently limit drawdown risk (Exhibit 19). Most equity bear markets coincide with a US recession — our economists’ US recession probability for the next 12 months is 20%, slightly above the unconditional level of 15%, mainly due to the weak labour market. However, while our economists’ macro baseline is particularly friendly in the first half of the year, macro momentum in the second half might increase downside risks. Also, there might be other drivers of equity drawdown risk, such as geopolitical shocks and concerns about AI disruption for software stocks, which might result in more frequent corrections. However, such corrections tend to be short-lived and thus difficult to time (Exhibit 20). And even though bear market drawdowns tend to be deeper and longer, the average profile of an S&P 500 >20% drawdown since 1900 shows that investors who divested 6 months before the peak roughly lost as much as those who were 6 months late. records.text: FOCUS F O C U S 09/02/2026 1 Japan: LDP landslide paves way for fiscal expansion Source: BNP Paribas Fig. 1: Number of seats in Japan’s House of Representatives Two-thirds majority for ruling coalition: Japan’s lower house election held on Sunday ended in a historic landslide victory for the LDP. The party captured 316 seats, an increase of a 118 seats from its pre-election tally and more than two-thirds of the 465-seat chamber. It is the first time since the post-war era that a single party has secured more than two-thirds of the seats on its own. With the seat count of coalition partner Japan Innovation Party (Ishin), rising to 36 seats (up two), the ruling alliance now holds 352 seats. The two-thirds super-majority means that the ruling bloc can now override any rejection of a regular bill in the upper house by passing the measure again in the lower house. In contrast, the Centrist Reform Alliance, the new party created by the merger of the Constitutional Democratic Party and Komeito, won only 49 seats – less than a third of the 172 seats the two parties together held before the election. The tally of the Democratic Party for the People stayed essentially flat at 28 seats (up one from 27), while that of the Sanseito grew from 2 to 15 seats – a modest gain compared with its surge in the July 2025 upper-house election. records.text: European Equity Strategy9 February 2026 ab 10  Energy Exposure: Producers of commoditized materials (e.g., standard steel/ concrete) that fail to use AI for energy optimization face margin erosion from volatile energy costs and carbon taxes Company Evidence  Aurubis: Positioned as a strategic enabler of AI infrastructure. They signed a long- term offtake agreement with Viscaria to secure copper concentrate, explicitly citing the "sharp rise" in demand from "data and AI centers" as a driver. This secures their position in the AI supply chain.  Merck: Their Electronics business is a key "AI Enabler," supplying the thin films and gases required for next-gen AI chips. They explicitly state that AI chips are "20% to 40% more material intensive," directly benefiting their bottom line.  Holcim: Uses AI and digital tools to drive its "circular cement" strategy (ECOCycle). After easing off pandemic highs through 2024, the pace of improvement in non-shelter services (NSS) inflation slowed in 2025. Currently, CPI NSS stands a bit above 3%, similar to where it was in H1 2025.2 We think this slowdown in service-side disinflationary progress is more signal than noise. First, while incremental labor slack can move the needle on services inflation at extreme levels of labor tightness, it packs less of a disinflationary punch once slack is closer to normal. Second, we think companies since the pandemic have become more comfortable using the price lever to boost nominal sales and smooth volatility in real activity. Third, services inflation embeds more inertia than goods inflation – both because pricing resets are less continuous and because measured services inflation is more exposed to imputation and smoothing. As a result, we think NSS inflation is more likely to hover around 3% than to glide back to 2% without a more meaningful cooling impulse. Labor market now provides less disinflation “bang for the buck”: Before the pandemic, NSS inflation remained low even as labor slack diminished, leading commentators to question whether the Phillips curve was dead. One big question for markets will be the impact of weight changes, as the ONS updates its consumption basket. In this weekly, we look at the potential effects of weight changes and what this would mean for the 2026 path ahead. How will the ONS update its CPI weights? The ONS will update the CPI weights for 2026 by re-basing them to 2024 household expenditure data (based on the detailed national accounts expenditure data). The ONS will then price update those expenditures to the latest price reference period (Dec-25), giving us a second slightly altered set of weights for 2026 (as part of a double-chain linking process). Importantly, unlike the structural weight changes taking place in the Euro-area as part of a bigger refresh of the COICOP structure, the ONS has delayed plans to transition to the new COICOP-2018 standards until early 2028. In effect, weight changes, we think, will be marginal this year. What kind of weight changes can we expect? records.text: US Rates Weekly 06 February 2026 Citi Research 6 The question now is: what does a potential Treasury Secretary Bessent / Fed Chair Warsh partnership look like? At a high level, Kevin Warsh can either: 1) reduce the balance sheet size via stopping some T-bill purchases and/or restart QT; or 2) reduce the WAM of the SOMA portfolio (see US Rates Weekly - New Year, New Fed Pick). The former is mechanically challenging due to last year’s repo stress. Three possible solutions could be: tiering of IORB as a function of reserve size, to push GSIBs to ‘spend’ reserves; ceasing paying IORB (this would require much debate); or utilizing SRPs (formerly SRF) to dynamically generate reserves as the sheet shrinks. On the latter, there should be broad agreement on the committee to rotate the UST coupons in SOMA into T-bills. This helps the Fed’s asset liability mismatch as they pay out an overnight rate and earn interest from the SOMA portfolio. At the same time, a higher T-bill share allows a future operation twist, reducing the need for a future QE program that would align with Warsh’s view on the sheet. See Alejandra’s section for further discussion on front-end impacts. The question is: does Treasury lean further on T-bills, pushing up T-bill share? records.text: are not laid off in January. After seasonal adjustment (which expects a larger swing from hiring to firing), the result is a boost to January payrolls. In our forecast, retail payrolls rebound from -25k in December to +30k in January. Transport and warehousing payrolls swing from falling to flat. In the other direction, we expect a 40k decline in federal government payrolls. The deferred resignation program (DRP), originally aimed at October resignations, appears to have been extended somewhat and perhaps enlarged somewhat. OPM Director Kupor indicated that about ⅔ of the resignations occurred in September, with the remaining ⅓ at the end of the year. We have also seen commentary that the total size of the program was somewhat larger than the 150k estimate. We've allowed 40k in layoffs in January simply because the October decline in federal government payrolls, -160k, was so large. There's risk in both directions for the federal government payrolls forecast: that for some reason the October payrolls report picked up the full DRP. Or that the program was larger than we recognized and resulted in more resignations at the end of December. In the one case, Federal employment decline could be near zero; in the other, as large as 70k. We estimate average hourly earnings rose 0.2% m/m, held back partially by the shift back toward lower-wage industry payrolls, with the y/y pace slowing 0.2 pct pt to 3.6%. The unemployment rate is unchanged at a 'low' 4.4%, after 4.375% in December.

records.text: Euro Area Outlook It's the data! The ECB continues to signal policy is in a "good place" , but "agile" . With inflation slightly below 2%, real GDP growing close to trend and historically low unemployment, data is now of less interest. However, it will be data that moves an agile ECB policy, and this week the data signal was dovish. • The ECB Governing Council (GC) unanimously decided to keep policy rates unchanged, with the deposit facility rate at 2.0%. The February meeting offered no new information to change our view on the most likely policy path or surrounding balance of risks. We still expect the ECB to remain on hold for the next two years, with risks tilted towards lower, not higher, policy rates over our forecast horizon. • Our risk assessment is dictated by our macro outlook. We forecast: (i) real GDP to grow at an average annual pace of 1.2% over our forecast horizon, a rate that we assess to be slightly above potential growth, and (ii) average headline inflation at 1.7% y/y for most of the coming two years. These forecasts are slightly below the ECB's December projections. Moreover, our latest reading of high frequency data points to slightly softer growth momentum and faster disinflation at the start of Q1 26 and than in Q4 25. • The dovish signals data provided this week are, we think, too small for the majority of the GC to even shift the tone of their communication. Challenges to monetary policy transmission A key challenge to maintaining the current monetary policy stance for an extended period lies in the still-underwhelming credit recovery and constraints this poses for the strengthening in investment that both we and the ECB expect over the coming quarters. The Q4 2025/Q1 2026 Bank Lending Survey (BLS) published this week did not alter this assessment (for more, see No respite for firms). While mortgage loan demand continued to expand at the end of 2025, the pace of growth appears to have slowed markedly, with banks reporting that the general level of interest rates is no longer supportive of household demand. The same diagnosis applied to corporates, where demand remained weak and was further constrained by subdued investment in fixed assets. Meanwhile, on the supply side, credit standards eased slightly for house purchases in Q4 2025 but tightened again for business loans, driven by concerns about the outlook for firms and the broader economy, as well as banks’ reduced risk tolerance. Previous ECB research has shown that BLS data exhibit leading-indicator properties for future lending growth, particularly for firms (Figure 5). Specifically, the cross-correlation between credit standards and annual loan growth is highest when the BLS leads actual loan growth by five to six quarters. Both headline and core inflation are already 20bp below the ECB’s 1Q26 forecast, and we expect the central bank’s hawkish projections to continue being disappointed. ECB: cuts will have to wait We had been warning that our conviction on an ECB cut in March was decreasing, given we thought January inflation would be a bit stronger than at the end of 2025. Data this week confirmed that and, hence, we take out the ECB cut in March-26. But the easing bias remains and in an explicit way. We now expect the ECB to cut policy rates in March and June 2027. Why that call? We have three strong convictions from here: 1. The ECB is more likely than not to cut; that comes from the asymmetry of risks we see for both growth and inflation. 2. We still think hikes are very unlikely, absent a shock, in the next two years. 3. One cut would make sense if delivered now, as a continuation of the cutting cycle. If the ECB doesn’t cut in the next few meetings there is no room for “insurance cuts” i.e. one and done, we think. records.text: Second part of report title TRADE IDEA TRADE IDEA 12/8/2026 US equity flow insights: On the surface, it looked calm for equities It was a wild route to SPX finishing almost exactly almost unchanged on the week. The pain trade was in equity factors and long/short. HF longs (BNPUSHFL) were down 5% on the week, and Software was down 9%. The beneficiaries of the rotation out of Tech, momentum and mega-caps were at the other end of the cyclical versus secular barbell: IWM +2%, XRT +4%, XHB +8% and KRE +7%. Staples +5% also led the Defensives, and INDU (an anachronistic quality cyclical play) quietly made a new all-time high >50k. Realized vol picked up off the lows, but 10d and 1m RV are still only ~15%. The VIX did acknowledge the undercurrents. records.text: More tariff pass-through in the pipeline: Our structural work on import cost shocks implies high ultimate pass-through into consumer prices and scope for second-round effects to amplify the initial shock (see US: Brace for second-round effects of tariffs on CPI, dated 6 February 2025). In practice, realized pass-through has been well below 100% so far. We estimate tariffs added about 0.3pp to CPI last year (roughly 40% of tariff costs). We interpret the gap as a pace story more than an amount story: firms appear to be passing through costs gradually - via selective list-price increases, reduced discounting, and product-mix changes - consistent with a demand backdrop where consumers appear more price sensitive. Our baseline is that this gradual cadence persists, keeping tariff-related pressure on goods prices through 2026. Two practical adjustments matter for the arithmetic. First, the tariff rate implied by collected revenues (the “effective” rate) has tended to undershoot the administration’s listed (“statutory”) rate (we outline the reasons for this in the following section). Our current estimate for the statutory rate is ~11.2% (as of January), which still points to a 0.8pp total addition to consumer prices under full pass-through. Second, sector heterogeneity - autos are the outlier. records.text: A Credit Rebound After a Decade-Long Deleverage In almost all Euro area countries, bank loans to the non-financial private sector have fallen as a share of GDP for the last 15 years. The reduction has been particularly sharp in Southern Europe, where loans had reached elevated shares of GDP until the Global Financial Crisis (GFC). The outstanding loans-to-GDP ratio in the region has fallen by more than half since the GFC. In core countries, loans have remained a relatively stable share of GDP (Exhibit 2). Since 2024 most Euro area member states have already started to experience a notable turnaround in bank lending growth. The increase has been the highest in Spain, Portugal and the Netherlands. Other member states, including Germany, France and Italy, have seen more modest gains but are also likely turned the corner (Exhibit 3). Second, the Bank removed a key sentence from the statement: “The ongoing inflation pressures from the domestic economy currently preclude a further decrease in interest rates. ” Third, the language on wage-driven inflation pressures was softened by removing the word “increased” from the sentence referring to above-average wage growth. records.text: Arguing for a stronger-than-expected report: Layoffs. The pace of layoffs—a particularly important determinant of net job n growth in January—was low this year. Initial jobless claims averaged 206k in the January payroll month vs. 218k in December, and the share of businesses reporting a decline in employment in January in the Business Trends and Outlook Survey was well below that of recent years (Exhibit 3, left). Announced layoffs by Challenger, Gray, and Christmas increased by 73k in January on a not-seasonally-adjusted basis, stoking concerns about an abrupt rise in layoffs. On a seasonally-adjusted basis, however, announced layoffs increased by just 8k and remained near the bottom-end of the range seen over the last year. End-of-year layoffs typically weigh on not-seasonally-adjusted January employment growth, and as a result, the seasonal factors expect a large decline in employment at the start of the year. While the low level of layoffs this January could argue for a boost to seasonally-adjusted job growth, end-of-year layoffs have been low over the past few years and the seasonal factors have evolved to expect smaller declines in employment in Januarys (Exhibit 3, right), limiting the scope for a boost from this channel. records.text: during the latter portion of 2025, argued this week that risks are now tilted toward higher inflation, with the labor market roughly in balance, suggesting that she favors retaining the current rate stance for some time. Although Richmond's Barkin (non-voter) made clear that he sees downside risks to both legs of the mandate, he emphasized above-target inflation, suggesting that activity could improve amid reduced trade policy uncertainty and more supportive fiscal and monetary policy. At the dovish end of the spectrum, San Francisco Fed President Daly (non-voter) made the case for additional cuts, mentioning that she was more worried about the labor market than inflation. Governor Miran (voter) argued that he doesn't "really see a lot of very strong price pressures in the economy” and that the FOMC would need to cut by more than 100bp this year. records.text: No return to 2010s calm: Our base case is for a step down in food inflation in 2026, but not a full reversion to the pre-Covid pace. We frame the recent food inflation trajectory as having moved from stable staples to serial idiosyncratic shocks. The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) has flagged weather, shifting trade patterns and crop diseases as recurring drivers of retail food price changes. We think a reasonable base case consistent with the USDA’s outlook is ~2.5% for overall food inflation in 2026, with food at-home and food away-from-home respectively in the 2% and 3% ranges. The structure of our forecast is that grocery prices normalize faster than restaurants. Food at-home – cooling continues but dispersion stays elevated: CPI food already shows a picture of uneven cooling. Food at-home inflation has eased but is still solidly above its pre-pandemic rate as some staple items run particularly hot. Meat, fish, and beverage prices were respectively up 9%, 4% and 5% in 2025, even as other items have fallen. Mechanically, dispersion makes sense to us for several reasons. Protein is supply cycle-dominated (biological lags, herd/flock dynamics, disease risk), while coffee, cocoa and sugar are globally priced and changes can reflect reasons that have little to do with domestic conditions. High scores reflect explicit revenue contributions, booked AI demand, or proven cost savings already flowing through the P&L. Middling scores indicate scaling pilots with early efficiency gains, while low scores flag companies that reference AI strategically but without quantification.  AI Risk Scores measure how vulnerable each company is to AI-driven substitution, margin pressure or regulatory friction. High scores flag business models where AI directly threatens the economic engine - such as labour-intensive services, legacy search/gatekeeping, or unprotected IP . Mid-range scores capture rising competitive pressure, compliance burden or litigation exposure. Low scores reflect largely manageable operational risks.  Evidence Strength ensures the scores remain grounded in verifiable disclosures, distinguishing between numbers disclosed in earnings reports versus qualitative commentary or third-party speculation. records.text: Regarding the consumption tax cut, the landslide victory of the ruling coalition, after having pledged this cut, has given it a mandate from voters. Although the scale and duration differ by party, the fact that most parties pledged a consumption tax cut means the likelihood of a cut on food items has significantly increased. However, changing the consumption tax rate requires approval from both houses of the Diet, so the ruling coalition still needs the cooperation of opposition parties to secure approval in the Upper House, where they do not have a simple majority. Prime Minister Takaichi has stated that she intends to discuss the funding and scheduling of a tax cut in a cross-party National Council and, if an agreement is reached, to submit related bills to the autumn Extraordinary Diet Session (this is consistent with our forecast that if a tax cut is implemented, it would be in April 2027). We expect discussions in the National Council to be based on the victorious ruling coalition’s proposal to reduce the tax rate on food items only to zero for two years, which we model would result in an annual tax revenue loss of about ¥5 tn (0.8% of GDP). We believe that as long as it is a two-year temporary measure, Japan’s fiscal position would not deteriorate significantly. However, restoring the consumption tax rate once it has been lowered would likely require considerable political effort, meaning there is a high risk that the cut would become permanent. The collapse stemmed from aggressive expansion, strategic errors, and a weakening macro environment. The acquisition of Air Deccan forced a high-cost, full-service operator into a low-fare market, eroding its premium brand and creating an unsustainable cost–yield imbalance. The fallout was extensive. Public sector banks were left with major unpaid dues despite government pressure to continue lending, while employees faced large-scale job losses and salary defaults. Passengers received no compensation for cancelled flights. Competitors, led by IndiGo, absorbed the vacated airport slots, accelerating market consolidation. records.text: End of shelter disinflation in sight: Shelter is in the late innings of a post- pandemic whipsaw. Rents surged initially as stay-at-home dynamics, remote work and fiscal support pulled demand forward and government support boosted both household formation and spending power.4 But cooling followed as the Covid shock faded and (critically) supply responded. That supply response is now doing its job. A multifamily construction wave has helped to nudge rental slack back toward pre-pandemic norms and pulled CPI rent inflation down. With rent inflation now around its pre-pandemic pace, the question is whether the market is near stabilizing or if any meaningful downside remains. We lean toward an expectation of limited further downside in rent inflation. While softer market rents point to a bit more incremental CPI rent disinflation this year, normalizing construction, broadly balanced rental vacancy, and solid income growth suggest that the scope of additional declines should be relatively modest. Put differently, we see a moderate amount of further cooling. As the post- pandemic supply impulse fades and fundamentals reassert themselves, we expect CPI rent inflation to bottom this year and edge back to a pre-Covid pace in 2027. records.text: M Foundation 16 What Is Really Going on with JPY Positioning? Here we are using 'JPY carry trade' in the sense of people exploiting interest rate differentials and low volatility by using borrowed JPY to purchase assets in foreign currencies for the purpose of generating higher yields. JPY has historically been favored by many as a funding currency for carry trades by virtue of Japan’s relatively low and stable interest rates. Some have contended that JPY carry trade activity has in fact been comparatively subdued, citing CFTC positioning data as pointing to much less of a JPY-short skew than in 2024 (see Exhibit 25 ). However, the FX futures trading activity captured by the CFTC data pales in comparison with FX spot market volumes (which obviously serves to limit utility as a measure of carry positions), and a look at the breakdown for the non-commercial sector is moreover indicative of (fleeter-footed) leveraged funds recently shorting JPY to roughly the same extent as in 2024 (see Exhibit 21 ). Hedge funds typically use derivatives such as FX forwards and options when executing (leveraged) JPY carry trades, in some cases opting for a 'cash settlement' approach (based on future differences in present value) and in others using FX swaps to borrow JPY, which is then sold in the spot market. More recently, performance has strengthened among likely AI adopters with valuable data, large customer bases, complex processes and high regulatory burdens - Banks, insurers, logistics operators, retailers and healthcare providers. BNP Paribas and Nordea are seeing margin expansion as revenue outpaces costs; DSV and Tesco report strong growth from AI scheduling and optimisation; and Siemens Healthineers is showing margin strength in imaging where AI supports diagnosis and reporting. Where AI disruption risk is most acute currently Market focus has recently centred on major AI coding advances that could threaten many software businesses—the MSCI Europe Software & Services Index has underperformed by 17% in the past month. Seat-based or labour-intensive providers without deep enterprise integration face clear pricing and demand deflation risk (eg. Teleperformance, Capgemini). In contrast, Europe’s largest software firm, SAP , sits inside core enterprise architecture, consolidating data and managing processes across divisions. It is seeing 30% cloud growth as AI accelerates migrations and expects €2bn in future cost savings. Stock selection is therefore essential to distinguish genuinely disrupted names from early AI adopters delivering irreplaceable enterprise services. The board replaced the December 18 forward guidance of “the Board will evaluate the timing for additional reference rate adjustments” with “the Board will evaluate additional reference rate adjustments, ” removing the phrase “the timing” . In our view, this tweak was implemented to signal that the bank would be willing to cut rates in March if inflation “behaves well” (ie, the effects of the shocks are weaker than expected). The staff’s inflation projections were updated, and the projected convergence to the 3% inflation target was postponed to Q2 27, from Q3 26. All in all, we still think Banxico will be able to deliver two 25bp cuts, in May and June, once the effects of the recent tax adjustments start to fade. This would leave the reference rate at 6.50%, where we expect it to remain for a long time. Core goods prices may be somewhat stronger than in recent months, with a 0.31% increase in our forecast, technically the strongest since 2023. This could reflect greater pass- through of tariff costs post-holidays at the start of the year, a natural time for prices to change anyway. But the most important details of January CPI will be various services prices. We expect further slowing in shelter inflation, with a modest 0.23% increase in owners’ equivalent rent and a 0.20% increase in primary rents. Even accounting for measurement issues, both OER and primary rents have experienced months of abnormally soft increases since September. While this slowing will not necessarily be consistent each month, we continue to expect softer than usual shelter inflation on average in 2026. Measurement – market rents point to a bit more disinflation: Market rent growth sagged through H2 2025, rolling over again late in the year after a modest midyear rebound. Directionally, that keeps the disinflationary signal intact. The pass-through, however, is neither immediate nor one-for-one. CPI rent (rent of primary residence (RPR) and owners’ equivalent rent (OER)) is dominated by continuing tenants whose rents reset episodically, typically at renewal. Market rent series largely capture new-tenant asking rents, in addition to having a shorter data series for comparison. On top of new-tenant asking rents versus mostly continuing-tenant renewals, CPI rent construction embeds deliberate smoothing: rents are collected in a rotating sample and convert six-month changes into a m/m price relative. records.text: 6 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 20 Deutsche Bank AG Seasonality Framework: In this section, we examine the seasonality patterns across a range of rates products with a focus on EUR rates. We split the calendar year to 24 half- month periods for which we estimate a seasonal signal. The data we analyze are demeaned (to neutralize for periods of persistently rising or falling rates or spreads), while we also exclude extreme data points by looking at the trimmed mean (20%) adjusted for standard deviation (stronger signal for variables with smaller standard deviation). Among other things, we look at the median change and the hit ratio. The combination of all these metrics leads to a seasonality score that is reflected in the colour-coded heatmap in our table. To determine the strength of the signal, we also look at the success rate of the seasonal signal achieved over the five most recent years. records.text: US Rates Weekly 06 February 2026 Citi Research 11 Relative Value: Swap flies and Jan inflation We highlight the attractive carry on 3y forward 5s10s30s swaps fly and reiterate our long belly position in the fly. January inflation prints have usually surprised to the upside, but we remain short in near-term inflation expectations. 3y 5s10s30s still looks attractive Despite the recent move lower, receiving belly in 3y 5s10s30s fly still looks attractive. In September of last year, we initiated a long belly position in 3y forward 5s10s30s fly to monetize the attractive risk-adjusted roll (see US Rates Weekly - Fed Funds Shutdown). Since then, the position has moved in our favor by about 9bp both due to the positive roll and 3y 5s10s30s moving lower by about 6bp (Figure 18). While the level of the 3y 5s10s30s fly is not at its historical highs, typically it has been hard for the fly to move significantly higher from current levels without the forward 10s30s curve flattening. The chances of the 3y fwd 10s30s curve flattening from here are pretty low, in our view, so we think it is still attractive to receive the belly in the 3y fwd 5s10s30s fly. The risk-adjusted roll-down still looks very attractive on the 3y 5s10s30s fly. While the spot 5s10s30s fly level is clearly lower than the historical relationship with the 5s30s curve would imply, forwards are not pricing this outperformance in the belly. records.text: 6 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 23 Eurozone and UK Sovereign Issuance: 09th Feb - 13th Feb Overview Strong supply continued in EGB primary markets this week, driven by second syndications from Italy and Belgium. Italy launched its new 15-year benchmark BTP Oct-41 for EUR 14 billion, and Belgium introduced its new 30-year benchmark BGB Jun-56 for EUR 6 billion. The week ended with total issuance at EUR of EUR 46.1 billion (EUR 46.3 billion in 10-year equivalent terms). Looking ahead, scheduled issuance for next week is estimated at EUR 21.7 billion (EUR 16.4 billion in 10-year equivalent terms), though the final number can always change due to syndications (for our syndications expectations, see our analysis in our EGBs 2026 outlook). Next week on Tuesday, Netherlands will begin the week's supply by issuing Green DSL Jan-44 for EUR 1.5-2.0 billion. Also on Tuesday, Austria will auction RAGB Feb- 31 & Feb-36 for EUR 1.7 billion, and Germany will auction OBL Apr-31 for EUR 5 billion. On Wednesday, Germany's second auction of the week will see the issuance of DBR Aug-54 & Aug-56 for EUR 2.5 billion. The same day, Greece is also scheduled to hold an auction for an estimated EUR 250 million; details will be announced next week. Wednesday will also feature Portugal's auction of PGB Jun-29 & Jun-36 for EUR 1.0-1.3 billion. Italy will conclude the week's supply on Thursday by auctioning BTP medium & long-term bonds for an estimated EUR 8.0-9.0 billion.

It approached 200bp in the second half of January, and there has been a clear upshift in the range. As the liquidity of inflation-linked JGBs is poor, a BEI of 200bp would indicate a level higher than that taking into account the risk premium. Looking at recent change, nominal interest rates and real interest rates have already moved in a proportion of four to one. Given the December rate hike and subsequent increase in nominal interest rates, the profitability of BEI positions has improved. However, upside has now finally become more limited, given the level, the prospect of a consumption-tax cut, and that the core CPI will in the foreseeable future slow to below 2% YoY. Implications for fiscal: We think such a BJT-led government is likely to bring much-needed stability to Thailand’s political landscape and economy. It ensures a degree of policy continuity without a dull period, and given Anutin had shown dynamism in the short five- month period since becoming prime minister last September, it may raise hopes for a quick roll-out of the BJT’s supportive policies (Figure 4). Thailand’s economic growth has been weak, and a strengthening THB has been weighing on exports and tourism. However, with a stable government likely to form, we expect the administration to be able to implement economic support measures, such as increased fiscal spending and cash handouts, to stimulate growth and alleviate pressure on businesses and individuals. This could a big change as the fiscal has been slow for the last few years. The prospect of increased fiscal and economic support also reduces the likelihood of rate cuts from the Bank of Thailand, in our view. The central bank has already cautioned that its policy space is limited, and further rate cuts may have limited effectiveness. The BJT's more pro- fiscal stance and ambitions to raise growth to over 3% will likely put pressure on the rates curve to bear steepen, we think. The key near-term offset is affordability concerns incentivizing the White House to avoid consumer-facing tariffs even as the headline rate stays unchanged. On the other side, we view AI diffusion as the clearest disinflationary structural risk, especially for services. The main uncertainty is implementation timing and pass-through: savings may show up first in margins and erode pricing power later. Our base case treats this as a medium-term downside risk, but faster diffusion of AI through the economy could pull that disinflation forward. KEY MESSAGES We expect US core inflation to remain broadly steady this year, holding near 3% as firm goods prices and sticky services inflation offset a cooling in shelter. We think services inflation drifts at an elevated level absent a shock, while tariff pass-through should prevent goods from being a clean disinflation anchor. Risks are two-sided. We see upside skew from cyclical strength and geopolitics, and downside from AI diffusion and potential tariff tweaks. records.text: 6 February 2026 Germany Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 6 Automotive production in Germany suffers from transformation, costs, and competition In addition to the energy -intensive sectors, the automotive industry ( -23% compared to its peak) experienced significant production declines. The net effect of the transformation in the industry towards electromobility is negative for production at German locations. It has also become obvious that the production of passenger cars in the volume segment in Germany has been scaled back for cost reasons. In addition, automotive suppliers, that primarily produce parts and components for internal combustion engine vehicles, had to reduce their capacities in Germany. From that perspective, the equity return picture over the next year continues to be a balance between the cyclical outlook and the valuation picture. Our US forecasts from here to the end of 2026 are for lower core inflation, range-bound bond yields, and a stable to slightly higher unemployment rate. Those cyclical factors alone imply a boost to one-year real returns of roughly 2pp in our models. But the high starting level of macro valuation implies a roughly 7pp drag on real returns. The full model which takes those valuation and cyclical drivers alongside a baseline real return suggests modestly positive one-year nominal returns of around 5%. That is a more modest equity return picture than the official forecasts by our Portfolio Strategy team, and we would not lean heavily on that estimate. Instead, it highlights the core tension between high valuations and a friendly macro environment that has been a longstanding feature of this cycle. Our simple macro-model-implied estimates could be too optimistic if the baseline level of return that we have assumed is too high. But they could also be too pessimistic. The metal content of consumption is lower and works mostly indirectly via production costs. These estimates suggest that the net inflationary effect of commodity price (as well as currency) trends over the past three to six months is negative (RHS figure), as the impact of higher metals prices is more than offset by lower agricultural prices. records.text: 6 February 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week in review ECB press conference The ECB left policy rates unchanged at 2%, with President Lagarde reiterating that monetary policy is "in a good place". The overall communication was one of constructive balance, with no clear directional signal for future policy moves . While the external environment remains challenging due to global trade tensions and the past appreciation of the euro, the domestic economy is showing resilience. This is supported by low unemployment, solid private sector balance sheets, and increased spending on technology, defence, and infrastructure. The recent dip in HICP inflation to 1.7% in January, below the ECB's Q1 forecast, was downplayed by President Lagarde, who expressed confidence that inflation will reach its target in the medium-term and suggested focus should not be put on any single data point. The risks to the outlook were described as broadly balanced. Upside risks to growth now include the adoption of new technologies like AI and deeper integration of the EU's Single Market. On inflation, higher energy prices were noted as a new upside risk, while the potential for increased exports from countries with overcapacity, such as China, remains a downside risk. Despite some constructive and hawkish elements in the press conference, the Governing Council is comfortable with the current policy stance and continues to favor a data- dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach. A BoK research paper published last December estimated South Korea’s potential growth would continue moderating in the years ahead, which could imply a lower real neutral interest rate – and in our view means long-end yields should be lower. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

Political stability has increased following the election. In addition, the Sanseito and the Democratic Party for the People (DPP) also increased their number of seats. In contrast, the Centrist Reform Alliance (CRA) saw a substantial loss of seats. Other factors contributing to the liberal camp's defeat include the failure of the CRA's "centrist" philosophy to gain traction, especially among younger voters. In our view, the Takaichi administration recognises the need for the impact of its expansionary fiscal policy on inflation and exchange rates to be offset by a certain degree of monetary tightening. Given this economic and political backdrop, we expect the Bank of Japan to somewhat accelerate the pace of rate hikes. In most Euro area countries, bank loans have fallen as a share of GDP for the last 15 years, recovering only recently and mostly where economic growth has been relatively more resilient. Since 2024 Spain, Portugal and the Netherlands have already experienced a notable increase in bank lending. Other member states, including Germany, France and Italy, have seen more modest gains but are also likely turned the corner. After controlling for financial conditions and lending standards, we look at the n relationship between economic growth and bank loans to the business sector and households in the Euro area. We find that GDP growth has a frontloaded impact on household loans while it takes a couple of quarters to build credit growth to the non-financial corporate sector, although the effect is persistent. At a cross-country level, we find that the impact of GDP on household loans is n especially frontloaded in Germany and France, while it is lower but more persistent in Iberia. Commodity Markets Are Small Diversification flows of investors can drive very large short-run commodity price increases because commodity markets are small versus investor portfolios, dominated by the large equity and bond markets. Open interest in the global copper market is ~135 times smaller than the amount of outstanding privately owned US Treasuries (Exhibit 3).4 If investors buy futures believing that commodity markets will tighten significantly in the future or provide significant hedging value against tail risks, futures prices can rise above fundamentals. While futures selling by commodity producers can dampen the price boost from investor buying, the net short-run price boost can still be very large if inflows from investors with deep pockets dwarf corporate hedging flows (as has happened since 2025 in the platinum and palladium rallies (Exhibit 1)). 3 Index investors have little, if any, impact on prices because index investors pursue commodity allocations for strategic diversification, and are effectively paid to take risk off the balance sheet of commodity producers, who derive little benefit from holding price risk. Meanwhile, the pattern of USD/JPY selling pressure during Asian hours appears consistent with foreigners buying Japanese equities without FX hedges (which mechanically involves buying JPY). Even so, our overall impression is that the latest bout of JPY depreciation has been driven more by forces other than straightforward securities investment flows. In our view, speculative JPY shorting – particularly during London and New York afternoon hours – has played a meaningful role in JPY weakness. CFTC positioning is not a comprehensive measure of overall carry activity, but it does suggest that leveraged funds have accumulated JPY short positions. In addition, several lagging indicators – such as the BIS International Banking Statistics and OTC derivatives data – point to a recent upswing in yen carry trades. We believe that concerns about fiscal expansion under the Takaichi administration led to such JPY short speculative positioning, and JPY weakness itself has been pushing inflation expectations higher and intensifying concerns that the BoJ is normalizing policy too slowly. As a result, medium-to-long-term JGB yields have increasingly incorporated a 'behind the curve' risk premium, with term premiums widening.

We think these options include letting MBS holdings roll off SOMA, decreasing the pace of reserve management purchases (RMPs), stopping RMPs, or restarting QT. While we can’t rule out any of these outcomes, it is likely that Warsh will prioritize getting committee consensus for cutting rates before aiming to reduce the balance sheet. We think the bar for restarting QT is quite high given the large volatility that repo markets experienced last year. The landslide victory also creates a sizable cohort of newly elected MPs who are likely to back her agenda. records.text: 6 February 2026 Germany Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 5 Energy-intensive sectors heavily affected These factors have left deep marks on domestic production statistics. Figure 4 shows how sharply manufacturing in important industrial sectors in Germany has shrunk in 2025 compared to its respective historical peak (measured by the real production index). These sectors are particularly feeling the impact of high energy prices compared internationally, as well as the increase in energy prices compared to the level prior to the war in Ukraine. Concerns about the future security of energy supply also play a role. For example, sectors with high gas consumption (e.g., chemicals) are affected by the fact that German net gas imports have fallen in recent years. The lower physical avai lability of gas, in addition to the price effect, has dampened domestic production. Manufacturing in the building materials industry also suffered from low demand due to the recession in German residential construction. Riksbank: No more cuts, policy rate at 1.75% The Riksbank left the policy rate unchanged at 1.75% in January and confirmed that it expects the policy rate to remain there "for some time to come”. However, the meeting minutes conveyed a more dovish message. This and the weak January inflation print led the markets to swiftly price in a 50% chance of a 25bp rate cut by June. Our baseline remains that the easing cycle has ended and the policy rate has bottomed at 1.75%. records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 06 February 2026 5 Australia in Focus Nick Stenner, CFA Merrill Lynch (Australia) Johnny Liu, CFA Merrill Lynch (Australia) See note: Australia Viewpoint: Fiscal pulse: Cyclical strength vs structural slippage Fiscal support meets monetary restraint Public demand growth likely eased to around 2.2% y/y in 4Q ’25, after the strong 5.6% expansion in 2024 that had been the main driver of GDP growth. Looking ahead, we expect private demand to continue expanding solidly through 1H ’26, while public demand growth rebounds toward roughly 3.0% in 2026. Despite slower growth in public outlays, public spending remains around a record high at 29% of GDP. Persistent structural spending pressures, most notably the continued expansion of the NDIS and rising defence commitments, are growing faster than nominal GDP. Positive fiscal impulse supporting growth in FY25-26 While the cyclical upswing underway, supported by historically low unemployment and elevated commodity prices, would normally point to a surplus, persistent structural spending pressures lead Treasury to project a $36.8bn deficit (1.3% of GDP) in FY25 26, widening from the $10bn deficit in FY24 25. The fiscal impulse assesses how expansionary or restrictive the fiscal stance is by adjusting for the business cycle and automatic stabilizers. We estimate a positive fiscal impulse will provide a growth tailwind in 2025-26, as the structural (i.e. cyclically adjusted) budget deficit is set to decline by 0.9ppt

records.text: Copper: Upside Risk From Positioning and the Commodity Control Cycle Copper has already benefited and may benefit further from the hard assets rotation as it combines constrained supply, an attractive long-run demand outlook, and ease of storage. That said, measures of active investor positioning have recently moderated even if prices stay elevated (Exhibit 8). While we are long-term bullish copper (with a $15,000/t forecast for 2035), our near-term base case remains that the LME copper price moderates from $12,994/t to $11,200/t by 2026Q4 because prices have overshot our estimate of fair value. This fair value estimate is based on ex-US inventories (because LME prices are set in London), which declined in 2024 (as anticipation of potential US tariffs pulled copper in the US) but have recently built, as China copper demand has softened. We next estimate the upside risks to our 2026Q4 copper forecast from a potential rise in positioning on the hard assets rotation in 3 steps. First, we estimate a short-term boost to copper prices from a 1pp increase (0.1 standard deviation) in net managed money as % of open interest of 0.7% (Exhibit 9). This is equivalent to a 6.9% short-term copper price boost from a 1 standard deviation year-over-year change in positioning. records.text: US Rates Weekly 06 February 2026 Citi Research 7 One concern Treasury should have with leaning on T-bills is increased exposure to interest rate risk to a one-time shock in the future, similar to when the Fed hiked rates in 2022. For example, in Figure 11, we report the increase in T-bill interest expense of a 4% shift in FF in the future as a function of T-bill share and interest rate levels. We pick FY32 as debt will grow throughout time. We also report the percent change of total (coupon+bills) interest expense from the year prior. In our view, being overweight T-bill share brings too large of a future refinancing risk for Treasury. Putting this together, we think one possible option would be for Treasury to not lean into T-bill issuance. The reason is less private T-bill supply would allow the Fed to reduce the balance sheet. For instance, last year the Fed’s QT program was brought to an early end due to Treasury’s large T-bill supply. We had argued at the time that the speed of the issuance, combined with an unusually large TGA balance and the proximity to year-end, was making the repo event look worse than it was (see US Rates Weekly - 2026 Outlook – Battle for Accommodation). That view was vindicated this year given repo is now exceptionally calm even though reserve levels have not changed too materially. Notably, recent job gains in the sector have been concentrated among specialty trade contractors, signaling strengthening demand tied to data center construction (Exhibit 4). Risks remain, particularly from tighter immigration policies, which could constrain labor supply in an already stretched sector. But the balance of factors points to a solid pickup in construction activity and employment in 2026. Negative on Professional & Business Services: AI adoption The professional & business services sector has posted several consecutive months of job losses (Exhibit 3), even as wage growth has accelerated. This combination of shrinking employment alongside rising pay is consistent with a sector undergoing rapid AI adoption, where automation is reducing demand for lower pay, routine roles while supporting continued wage growth for the remaining, more specialized positions. The upcoming annual benchmark revisions are likely to reinforce this story. We expect job growth in the sector to be revised down further for April 2024 - March 2025, indicating that the restructuring associated with AI adoption began earlier and progressed more deeply than current data suggest (see report: US Economic Viewpoint: Jan jobs FAQs: The Super Bowl of jobs reports). records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Appendix Note on Percentiles We use percentiles to gauge the significance of a flow or positioning metric over a variety of time periods and countries. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. records.text: bilizing around full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse and consumer resilience. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 50k in 2026 after coming in at 15k in 2H25. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Hence, we see the u-rate ticking up to just 4.5% in 4Q25, where it should remain in 1H26 before dropping to 4.3% by 4Q26. Fed: two cuts in 2026 but on hold under Powell • The Fed held rates steady at 3.5-3.75% at the January meeting, as expected. In the characterization of current conditions, the Fed leaned into the Dec u-rate decline. Powell’s comments on the labor market mirrored the optimism in the statement. But he also highlighted some pockets of concern. We remain comfortable with our view that the Fed won’t cut again under Powell. We have penciled in two 25bp cuts under the next Chair, with low conviction, in June and July. Policy under the next Chair will depend a lot on the composition of the FOMC. This leaves our projection of the terminal rate unchanged at 3.0-3.25%.

records.text: 23 2024 2025 2026 Source: Refinitiv, Morgan Stanley Research Our price forecast In our view, the market is still underappreciating the risk of Indonesian export cuts. While we do not see Indonesian coal production falling to 600 Mt, we still think there will be material declines in production YoY. We do not expect the market to feel the full impact of our 90 Mt cut to Indonesian exports YoY, as this will partly be offset by weaker Chinese import demand under higher prices. Policy relaxation remains a key risk; however, our modelling already assumes that cuts will be smaller than announced targets. We now see the market tighter by ~18 Mt vs our previous estimate for the 2026 balance, forecasting the balance to be in a 9 Mt deficit this year. We consequently flag moderate upside to our current Newcastle 6000cv 2026 price target of $116/t, as higher grade coals should also benefit from Indonesian export cuts. For NEWC6000 prices to move all the way to our 2026 bull case of $150/t, we believe we would need to see FY production in Indonesia fall to the government's ~600 Mt target and for Chinese import demand to remain relatively resilient even under higher prices. This could potentially happen if the Chinese government keeps tight controls on growth in China's domestic coal production, as they pursue anti-involution policies in the sector. However, we still see this outcome as relatively unlikely.

AI projects need to be funded at the same time governments are running sizable fiscal deficits. Even though most developed economies are dealing with high fiscal deficits and market pressure on public debt while the AI revolution is happening mostly in the US, financial markets are highly integrated and therefore global portfolios need to decide how to allocate credit between public and private pockets. And markets test governments from time to time. We have seen it in the UK, now it is more notable in Japan, and of course in the US, the most important market in terms of size and liquidity. Although the fiscal problems are global in nature, Japan and the US are currently the most sensitive. Different from Japan, the US is “managing” the long end of the curve, increasingly issuing short term paper to avoid more pressure in the long end of the curve. records.text: rch estimates, Bloomberg, Federal Reserve Even returning to an all-Treasury portfolio will take time. With mortgage rates having risen dramatically since 2022, prepayment speeds have dropped sharply, significantly slowing passive runoff. We loosely estimate that mortgage rates may need to fall by roughly 100bp from current levels to increase monthly prepayment speeds by $5bn/month at the Fed's current amount of mortgage holdings. Given that mortgage run-off will slow down as the portfolio gets smaller due to denominator and selection bias effects, we estimate it would take about 8 years for the Fed's portfolio to be cut in half to "just" $1tn. In other words, cutting agency MBS holdings in half through passive runoff alone would likely take close to a decade, even if we assume a substantial decline in mortgage rates to revive refinancing activity. Because active MBS sales would likely widen spreads, depress liquidity, worsen housing affordability, and lead to mark-to-market losses, the Fed continues to have strong incentives to avoid asset sales. Treasury Coordination Shrinking the balance sheet modestly without altering reserves is possible, but would require coordination with Treasury. The TGA has ballooned to nearly $1tn after the financial crisis and COVID. Cutting the TGA in half could allow the Fed to reduce its securities holdings and still leave the Treasury with a large cash buffer. With positioning so stretched, it is difficult to sustain rallies without correction. But with fundamentals still solid and no changes in the main macro drivers of momentum, we would buy the dip, while using value as a hedge. We are a bit more in favour of EU over US momentum, as while higher US tech capex can weigh on the latter, it’s one of the main drivers of some of the momentum upside in Europe. records.text: 1. Re-routing and substitution: Companies have adjusted supply chains toward lower-tariff sourcing where possible. Imports to China are down around 30%. 2. Carve-outs and exclusions: Negotiated deals and administrative exclusions have shrunk the taxable base, even as headline tariff programs remain in place. 3. USMCA compliance reality check: We (and government agencies) likely underestimated the share of imports from Canada and Mexico that is USMCA- compliant (and therefore effectively tariff-exempt). Muted tariff revenues are consistent with higher compliant shares, which mechanically lowers the effective statutory rate relative to earlier assumptions. Flipping signs: The establishment of the WTO and NAFTA in the 1990s helped lower costs and push goods inflation structurally lower. From 1995 to 2019, goods inflation was essentially nil. A return to that regime is far from assured. In the near term, goods inflation could run structurally higher over the next several years as firms continue to gradually pass tariffs through to consumers and navigate supply-chain restructuring. records.text: 6 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 51 Drivers of 10y UST in a low vol environment The 10y UST yield can be loosely decomposed into three components: terminal rate pricing, term premium, and the 10y swap spread. Our 10y yield forecast is built explicitly around views on each of these drivers. Historically, terminal rate pricing has been the most dominant driver, outweighing the other two by a significant margin. In recent weeks, terminal pricing has moved into a narrower range of ~3.10%– 3.30%, while term premium and swap spread have exhibited greater volatility. To quantify the impact on 10y yields, we scale each factor's realized volatility by its regression coefficient estimated against the 10y yield. The resulting metric captures each factor's economic impact on the 10y yield in bp terms. The ordering of importance has not changed: terminal pricing remains the primary driver, followed by term premium and then swap spread. That said, the degree of dominance has waned, with terminal pricing exerting less influence and swap spread playing a larger role in driving the moves in 10y yields. In short, the Fed still anchors the 10y, but swap spreads are doing more marginal work in today’s low- volatility environment. records.text: 12 Fig. 27: VAR outputs and BNP Paribas forecast Note: Series modeled through Q3 2025 to avoid government shutdown-related Q4 2025 volatility Sources: BLS, Census Bureau, NAR, BNP Paribas Modeling CPI rent with a VAR: To quantify the MAPS intuition, we start with a simple structural regression: CPI rent is related to labor slack (unemployment gap), wage growth, rental vacancy, and home payments as a share of income (an affordability proxy). These variables explain a meaningful share of variation in CPI rent – roughly 70% for RPR and 80% for OER – even without own-lags, suggesting these variables capture the structural drivers of CPI rent. We then estimate a vector autoregression (VAR) model and a structural VAR (VARX) in which we input our baseline forecast for labor slack and wage growth. We treat both models as sanity checks on direction and magnitude, rather than as mechanical forecasts. The headline result is that both the VAR and the VARX do not point to a deep cooling episode in shelter. The implied profile is consistent with a glide, with the model troughing around mid-to-late 2026, broadly aligning with the signal from the distributed lag market rent model. The trough is also relatively shallow. For blended CPI RPR-OER, the model suggests a trough around 2.9-3.1% q/q saar – a slight dip from current levels. How would sustained investor diversification into hard assets in an uncertain world affect commodity prices? Large Boosts. Investor diversification flows can drive large short-run price n boosts because commodity markets are small vs. equities and bonds. We see greater price upside from the hard assets rotation for precious metals and copper than for oil and natural gas for three reasons. #1. Market size. Investor diversification flows can boost prices more in metals n markets, which are (very) small. #2. Supply response. Higher energy prices incentivize shale supply, which in turn n dampens the price boost from investment flows. In contrast, supply is particularly constrained and largely long-cycle for copper and especially precious metals. #3. Storage. Higher supply and lower demand result in inventory accumulation n until hitting storage capacity limits (which are lower for energy than for metals) which can trigger large roll costs for energy futures. In contrast, roll costs remain limited on futures for easy-to-store metals, and don’t exist when owning physically backed assets such as precious ETFs. Gold. records.text: The Hard Assets Rotation Implies Greater Upside For Metals Energy and agriculture historically tend to perform well when large unexpected inflation shocks hit for two reasons. First, energy/food supply disruptions often cause inflation spikes. Second, demand for energy and food (key necessities) tends to remain robust even when inflation-adjusted incomes drop. However, precious metals and copper have already benefited more and could see greater price upside than oil and natural gas from a hard assets rotation, driven by market concerns about future macro policy, geopolitical or inflation shocks for three reasons. Factor 1: Market Size A given volume of investor diversification flows can boost prices more in metals markets, which tend to be small or very small in the case of the ex-gold precious markets such as silver, platinum, and palladium, which have rallied sharply since 2025 (Exhibit 1). Factor 2: Supply Response Higher energy prices incentivize short-cycle shale supply, which in turn dampens the price boost from investment flows. In contrast, supply is particularly constrained and largely long-cycle for copper and especially precious metals. Gold supply doesn’t feature in our demand-driven framework explaining gold prices. The reason is that the above-ground stock edges up at a very modest and stable pace because this stock dwarfs annual mine production, which is stable, and largely unresponsive to price (Exhibit 4).
