Structural shift could reform the semiconductor cycle: Over past 30 years, global semiconductor demand has progressed through distinct phases. ▪ 1995–2010: Growth was driven primarily by PCs and consumer electronics. ▪ 2011–2023: Boom in smartphone-upgrade cycle became a dominant catalyst. ▪ Since 2024: AI-driven computing has taken the lead. This evolution has shifted the predominant ultimate end-user from individual consumers to corporates, which tend to adopt a more systematic approach to financial planning and demand forecasting. On wages, the upside surprise in compensation per employee in Q3 was driven by wage drift, not base wages. By the next meeting, the ECB will have information on Q4 negotiated wages (20 February) and compensation per employee (6 March), which should be important in determining the directionality of the risk compared with the current services inflation forecasts. As alluded to above, the January flash HICP release this week was marginally soft, with headline easing 0.3pp, to 1.7% y/y, but core printing below consensus at 2.2% y/y (-0.1pp vs. December). Energy base effects dragged down the headline, while a deceleration in services inflation (3.2% y/y, -0.2pp) brought down core. The breakdown from German state data indicates the softness may have come from services that reset at the beginning of the year and normally change little for the rest of the year. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 The Broadening Accelerates Despite choppiness across large cap indices last week, our broadening thesis continued to play out with cyclicals leading the way, and the S&P Equal Weighted Index making new highs on Friday. In particular, we were encouraged by significant outperformance from early cycle reflation trades including Transports (+9% last week), Housing (+8%), Regional Banks (+7%), and Small Caps (+4%). We continue to like these areas of the market, which align with our "run it hot" framework. From a macro standpoint, it's worth highlighting that last week's ISM Manufacturing PMI reading was the strongest since 2022. This comes on top of an already established uptrend in industrial production. See our prior work for more on why we think an ISM re-acceleration is likely this year. Earnings momentum is the key driver of the broadening we're seeing. Earnings growth for the median stock in the Russell 3000 is +11% Y/Y, which is the strongest growth in 4 years. Our highest frequency gauges of earnings revisions breadth have risen shaprly over the past 3 weeks across both the S&P 500 and S&P 600 Small Cap Index. The S&P Small Cap Index is seeing its best revisions breadth since August (+7%) and its strongest EPS growth since 2022 (+10%). Further, it just made a new relative high versus large caps last week. US policy uncertainty remains high, but outside the US the data are slowly improving, and global confidence is inching higher (the caveat is that all our tracking estimates predate the geopolitical tensions over the last few weeks). Policy is turning more supportive this year, with several major advanced economies expected to benefit from fiscal stimulus, and policy rates now back to close to neutral in most economies. AI’s footprint is visible everywhere, and still driving almost all of US investment growth, half of global trade growth and the bulk of equity returns. records.text: Oil: Upside Risk From Positioning and Geopolitics While we see metals as a cleaner expression of the hard assets theme than energy, our investor conversations suggest that the hard assets rotation has contributed to the year-to-date rise in active investor oil positioning from low levels along with related geopolitical uncertainty. While our long-run crude oil price forecast is above the forwards (Brent 2030 forecast of $75), our near-term base case remains that Brent moderates from $68/bbl to a bottom of $54 by 2026Q4 for two reasons. First, we expect a 2026 surplus of just over 2mb/d assuming the January supply disruptions in Kazakhstan and the US ease and no large new supply disruptions (if US policymakers focus on affordability). Second, we assume that the share of global inventory increases in the OECD commercial pricing centers picks up from its unusually low just under 10% share in 2025 to the historical norm of ~30% (as the pace of accumulation of sanctioned barrels on water moderates). We next estimate upside risks to our oil price forecast, including from a potential rise in positioning, in 3 steps. First, we estimate a short-term boost to oil prices from a 1pp increase in net managed money as % of open interest of 3.7% (Exhibit 12). This is equivalent to a 10% short-term oil price boost from a 1 standard deviation year-over-year change in positioning. records.text: M Update 4 Next Week: GDP in EA, UK & Norway Euro area | A fairly quiet week in EA data space: There are few data releases next week, after a busy start to the month with the January HICP inflation print and the ECB Governing Council. The main focus will be on the second estimate of 4Q25 GDP for the euro area, due on Friday, which we expect to be in line with the preliminary flash estimate (0.3%Q). The release comes with the first estimate for employment, which we think slowed down to 0.1%Q in 4Q25, from 0.2%Q. On Wednesday we get the ECB's Wage Tracker, where we look for confirmation that negotiated wage growth is expected to hover around 2.5%Y in 2026. IP in Italy for December is expected to decline (-0.7%M) following a strong rise in November, and in line with drops observed in Germany, France and Spain on that month. On the policy side we will hear from ECB's Lane, Schnabel, Nagel, Cipollone, Radev, and Stourmas. Scandi | Norwegian focus: Next week brings 4Q GDP and the January inflation print, both of which are key for our Norges Bank rate call. We expect 4Q GDP at 0.3%Q (below NBe: 0.5%Q), supported by household consumption. However, industry and offshore sector should be a drag. On inflation, we expect CPI at 2.9%Y (from 3.2%Y) and CPI-ATE at 2.7%Y (from 3.1%Y). While CPI should come in above Norges Bank's forecast (due to electricity prices), we expect core to be weaker due to annual services repricing (including rents) coming in lower, and food inflation base effects

records.text: ld be the first increase in industrial production since 2021 and only the second since 2019. Our cautious optimism is based, among other things, on sentiment indicators in the manufacturing sector, which are tending to improve despite some volatility (except for employment expectations). Capacity utilization has also passed its low point despite a small decline at the beginning of 2026. There is a chance that the expected increase in production this year can continue in 2027, because fiscal policy will continue to provide impetus then too and could gain broader impact. For a lasting strengthening of Germany as an industrial location beyond the next two years, however, structural reforms are absolutely necessary. A longer -term look back at the development of the manufacturing sector in Germany shows that this is necessary. We show how sharply production in important industrial sectors in Germany has shrunk in 2025 compared to its respective historical peak . In the entire manufacturing sector , production in 2025 was 1 5% below its peak (2018). The data shows that the expected recovery in industrial production in 2026 and 2027 would by no means offset the losses of previous years. Without structural reforms, a return to previous production levels is hardly possible. records.text: M Foundation 6 How Do Investors Interpret the Recent JPY Weakness? In our conversations with clients, we sense that JPY has represented the intersection of various global and local themes observed in the past few years – fiscal dominance, the return of inflation, and demand for carry trades. Fiscal dominance: Investors often talk about the long-run challenges associated with DM economies and their large and rising stock of on- and off-balance sheet obligations. Put simply – debt and deficits are high and political will to lead to more fiscally sustainable outcomes is low. In fact, in many cases over the past few years political leaders have veered in the other direction. Rising risk premium around the fiscal outlook was already a key theme in the UK in 2022 and France in more recent years. The weakening of JPY alongside more term premium in the bond market as local political leaders debate more fiscal expansion aligns well with what investors consider to be a key long-term theme. The return of inflation: Covid represented a sea change in inflation paths globally. Instead of persistently below-target inflation rates that led central bankers to pursue unconventional policies as they faced the effective lower bound, inflation rates globally have generally exceeded targets. For foreign investors, the BoJ's battle against deflation was generally viewed as one of the most difficult but also the one where the most action was taken. records.text: 6 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 52 Deutsche Bank AG Commodities & HICP inflation Volatility in commodity prices has been relatively high in recent months, with divergent underlying trends across markets. Energy prices for example have risen noticeably since the start of the year, but this follows a gradual move lower through the second half of 2025, with Brent currently broadly at the same levels as last summer, while natural gas prices remain well below mid-2025 levels 3 . Metal prices, however, have continued to move higher, and are still up almost 5% this year, despite the recent correction. Agricultural prices, finally, have on average trended lower in recent months. To assess the net impact of these trends on the euro area inflation outlook, we look at input-output tables to estimate the commodity content of consumer goods and services 4 (replicating earlier work done for the US). The agricultural goods content of consumer spending is relatively high (LHS figure), consistent with the comparatively elevated weight of food items in HICP as well as the importance of food products as inputs for restaurant services. In the current context, the downward pressure from global agricultural prices is likely to be amplified by weakness in EU farmgate prices, which are down >7% over the past six months. The oil content of consumer spending is estimated at over 3%, reflecting its importance (i) for HICP petrol and liquid fuel components and (ii) as an industrial input

SpaceX / xAI merger - a vertical integration play, and a means of addressing xAI cash burn Earlier this week SpaceX announced its acquisition of xAI – a development that followed reports late last week that SpaceX was considering a merger with either Tesla or xAI1 . The SpaceX/ xAI merger will be the largest of all time, creating an entity value at $1.25tn ($1tn SpaceX, $0.25tn xAI). While the merger came as somewhat of a surprise, we see the logic behind it. In the announcement, Elon Musk, CEO of both companies, noted that the merger would create a "vertically-integrated innovation engine, " with plans to launch space data centers to satisfy the compute needs of AI models on earth, all connected through SpaceX's network of Starlink satellites. records.text: Peak tariff rate in the rear-view mirror: The latest US–Taiwan trade agreement, lowering Taiwan’s ‘reciprocal’ rate from 20% to 15%, increases our confidence that the overall, effective (i.e. collected) tariff rate imposed on Taiwan will not move any higher from where it stood in November 2025 (latest available data). Undershoot: Taiwan is among the US trading partners whose effective tariff rate has reportedly undershot the statutory (i.e. announced) rate by the largest degree (Financial Times, 8 October 2025). Our own estimates, using 2024 bilateral trade values, show the reduction in the ‘reciprocal’ rate reduces the overall, statutory rate to 8.6%, but it remains comfortably above the latest effective rate of 3.9%. This may not be an implementation issue. Tectonic shifts in the composition of US– Taiwan trade last year mean more than 80% of US imports from Taiwan (mainly electronics) are now exempted from tariffs, versus below 45% in Trump’s first term (Figure 16). Accounting for such shifts puts the latest statutory rate at 3.9%, right in line with the effective rate (Figure 18). After all, US tariff collection from Taiwan has had nine months of data to close the gap with a theoretically higher statutory rate – and it has not. What’s more, higher frequency data through December 2025 and January 2026, of overall rather than bilateral US tariff collection, reinforces our view that the rate has peaked (Figure 17). 8 Sources: US Census Bureau, Macrobond, BNP Paribas Fig. 18:

Understandably, tariff risks loom large on regional economies after the Liberation Day and esp. when US and China raised tariff rates to exorbitant levels for each other in April. Against this backdrop, Asia CBs eased overall policy stance to support growth, but in a calibrated manner to preserve space to respond to additional downside risks. These include a change in tones from RBA, BoK, MAS, BoJ and BSP. Figure 2: Baseline three-year lookback FCI-G Figure 3: Alternative one-year lookback FCI-G Source: FRB, Haver Analytics, Deutsche Bank Source: FRB, Haver Analytics, Deutsche Bank Figures 2 and 3 show our daily FCI-G indices for the baseline three-year lookback and alternative one -year lookback versions as well as how they line up with the Fed's monthly series. Both indices remain very easy, and, via the Fed’s internal models, would be expected to add around a percentage point to the growth outlook over the next four quarters. Financial conditions this easy likely make Fed officials slightly less concerned about a sharp deterioration on the employment side of their mandate , especially when paired with recent preliminary signs of stabilization in the labor market data. The tightening in financial conditions over the last week would either need to be sustained for a meaningful length of time or show signs of impacting market functioning for the Fed to begin signalling their concern about financial conditions. records.text: her the Phillips curve was dead. As the labor market tightened and NSS inflation surged post-pandemic, commentary shifted to the Phillips curve being reanimated and how much slack would be needed to pull NSS inflation back to target-consistent levels. Beningo and Eggertsson, 2023, propose that a non-linear Phillips curve explains this phenomenon. Inflation becomes more sensitive to labor market tightness only when slack is at extreme levels; at more normal levels of slack, the relationship weakens significantly. In their framework, the curve looks more like an “inverted- L” than a smooth slope. The authors use the ratio of job vacancies to unemployment (V/U) – a standard tightness metric in matching models – and find the inflation-slack relationship is much stronger once V/U rises above about 1. Below that threshold, inflation is only weakly related to labor slack. These dynamics appear at play with NSS inflation, which we plot against V/U in Figure 10. The implication is that the cooldown in labor-market tightness from extreme levels helped pull NSS inflation down from its peaks. But with slack now closer to normal, the labor market has provided less incremental disinflation – consistent with a slowing of disinflation – suggesting that a larger cooling-impulse may be needed to pull NSS inflation back to 2%. 5 Dashed line is BNP Paribas forecast. Understandably, tariff risks loom large on regional economies after the Liberation Day and esp. when US and China raised tariff rates to exorbitant levels for each other in April. Against this backdrop, Asia CBs eased overall policy stance to support growth, but in a calibrated manner to preserve space to respond to additional downside risks. Going into 2026, we predicted that most Asian central banks will continue to lean towards easing in our Year Ahead 2026 published in Nov. Narratives have shifted hawkish recently In the last two months, a more synchronized shift of monetary policy stance in the “hawkish” direction has emerged, as downside risks to the global growth outlook receded more meaningfully. records.text: tion approach, which in transition could map to supply-chain disruptions. 4) AI diffusion: AI is the clearest structural disinflationary force on the horizon, with the likely highest sensitivity in services. The channels are straightforward: faster productivity growth, automation of routine tasks and stronger competitive pressure as marginal costs fall. The uncertainty is less about sign than about timing and pass-through. If adoption is gradual and savings accrue first to margins, the CPI impact is a 2027-and-later story. But if diffusion is rapid and competition forces savings into prices, disinflation could arrive sooner and break the “sticky services” regime without requiring a recession, pulling non-shelter services inflation down sooner than our base case assumes. 5) Entrenchment – the regime risk: Entrenchment of inflation is a regime risk, where 3% becomes a de facto nominal anchor as companies and households adapt to repeated cost shocks that are passed through gradually, rather than absorbed. The risk is micro and behavioral – if pricing norms adjust to a world where demand tolerates recurring increases and repricing is episodic, inflation can remain persistent even as the cyclical impulse fades. records.text: What the lessons mean for investors First, China’s bifurcated economy allows for both bullish and bearish narratives, with each side able to find supporting evidence in the data. Therefore, investors should examine data carefully and comprehensively to get a full and accurate picture of the Chinese economy. For example, during the property market expansion in the 2010s, the official NBS Services PMI was typically stronger than the unofficial RatingDog Services PMI. Recently, however, this relationship has reversed as the property sector entered a sharp downturn (Exhibit 10). Just as one shouldn’t be overly optimistic about the Chinese services sector based solely on the RatingDog services PMI, it’s also important not to rely only on the NBS Services PMI and conclude that overall services activity is contracting. Second, in the prolonged process of economic restructuring, we believe the steepest declines in the housing market are behind us, and there are early signs that technological innovation is spreading to more industries. Investors may want to be open-minded about segments of the economy that have been depressed in recent years, as some of these areas could be bottoming out in the coming year. records.text: Gold: The Hardest Commodity Gold’s limited, slow-moving, price-inelastic supply is what has given gold its status as a neutral store of value and is also why gold is likely the cleanest commodity expression of the rotation in hard assets/private sector diversification theme. Private sector diversification is also the key upside risk to our $5,400 Dec26 forecast, which only assumes i) that central banks continue to buy at their elevated pace of the past 12 months and ii) a modest boost to ETF holdings from 50bp of Fed cuts. With gold ETF allocations in US private sector financial portfolios at only ~0.2%, there is room for additional diversification into gold. We estimate that every 1bp increase in the gold share of US financial portfolios—driven by incremental gold purchases—raises prices by 1.5%. (This diversification is increasingly expressed via call options, which has also boosted price volatility). Exhibit 7: We Estimate that Each 1bp Increase in Gold’s Share of US Financial Portfolios— Driven by Incremental Investor Buying—Lifts the Gold Price by About 1.5%. Annex This section includes some explanatory notes for our FCI. * In the Fed's construction of the FCI -G, the weights are derived from shocking variables in various macro models that are used at the Fed Board. Importantly, when shocking these variables, it holds all other variables constant, which is why decreases in the ten-year Treasury has the opposite sign than one might expect. A higher Treasury rate, holding other interest rates fixed, gives higher coupon payments to bondholders, which generates a slight positive income effect and would be considered an easing of financial conditions. We re-arrange terms in the Fed’s FCI formula to put things in the more typical formulation of mortgage and corporate spreads. This gives a more natural interpretation where a lower 10y eases conditions, but would be partially offset by wider spreads if those rates did not come down as well. While we think equity/bond correlations should be more negative in 2026, especially in ‘risk off’ episodes, the buffer from bonds might be smaller and Sharpe ratios during ‘normal’ markets might be lower going forward. We would expect equity/bond correlations to be more negative with markets less driven by monetary policy expectations and more by growth optimism since Q4. The S&P 500 has become more positively correlated with US 10-year breakeven inflation and less negatively correlated with real yields, indicating that investors are less concerned about monetary policy tightening (Exhibit 23). As we wrote before, equity/bond correlations tend to be structurally more negative on average with lower inflation as growth shocks become a more important driver relative to rate shocks (Exhibit 24) — our macro baseline with further inflation normalisation points to more negative equity/bond correlations. However, the buffer from bonds for large equity drawdowns might be smaller compared with the last 30 years. records.text: 10 US Economic Weekly | 06 February 2026 Core views Growth: a dose of optimism • Our 2026 average US GDP growth forecast of 2.8% is well above consensus (2.1%). The key drivers are easier fiscal and monetary policy, and our expectation of more growth-friendly trade policy. We now project that consumer stimulus from the OBBBA will be more front-loaded into tax season. This prompts us to tweak our forecasts: we modestly raise 1H 2026 growth and lower 2H. Risks to our projections are tilted to the upside. A 3-handle on 2026 growth wouldn’t be a big surprise. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We continue to expect inflation to remain above the Fed's target throughout our forecast horizon. In the near term, supply-driven inflation due to tariffs should push inflation above 3% y/y through 3Q 2026 as businesses continue to slowly shift costs to consumers. Inflationary pressures from tariffs should fade towards the end of 2026; however, core PCE inflation should end 2026 at an elevated 2.9% y/y and only decline to 2.4% by year end 2027. We continue to believe underlying inflation is above 2%, and our growth and monetary policy outlook should generate more demand driven inflation causing a delay in inflation’s return to the Fed’s 2% target. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real time information on consumer behaviour.
